sail-01.title: Safety before speed
concepts: A good departure starts with the crew, the weather and the boat, not the engine. Everyone wears a lifejacket that fits, knows where the emergency gear is, and knows how you will call for help and get a person back out of the water.

Before you leave, brief the crew and check the boat:
• Crew: the boom, which swings across when the boat turns and can knock a person overboard; things to trip on; where to hold on; and keeping hands clear of loaded lines and winches.
• Boat and plan: the forecast, local restrictions, radio and phone, fuel or battery charge, and that the boat is seaworthy (sound and fit for the trip).

Choose conditions that suit the least experienced person aboard, and agree in advance when you will turn back. This course builds understanding and some simulated skills; finishing it does not qualify you to skipper a real yacht.

Before a trip of several days, give the crew a fuller briefing:
• Going overboard: why it is dangerous and how to stay aboard.
• Jobs: what help you will need from each person. Ask them to tell you about anything that seems unusual.
• Fire: care with the stove and anything else that can burn.
• Leaving the boat: what to do if you must abandon it.
• Fragile equipment: how to use the toilet and other gear that is easy to damage.
observe: Before departure, tell your crew where to sit, how to move, and who will keep lookout.
Identify the boom and imagine its sweep across the cockpit.
sail-01.mistake: Starting because the weather looks pleasant without checking the forecast or briefing the crew.

quiz.prompt: A new crew member is aboard. What comes before departure?
options: Fit lifejackets and explain hazards, emergency equipment, and roles
Leave first and explain the controls underway
quiz.explanation: Prepare the crew and boat before getting underway; discovering a missing safety item after departure is too late.

quiz.prompt: What does passing this simulator course establish?
options: Understanding and selected skills in a simplified simulation
Readiness to sail alone in all weather
quiz.explanation: On-water instruction and assessment are still needed. The simulator omits many physical and environmental demands.

sail-01.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.
localNotes: Israeli regulations forbid throwing any rubbish or food waste into the sea, at any distance from shore. Keep it aboard and bring it back to harbor.

sail-58.title: Safety gear aboard
concepts: The safety gear a boat must carry depends on its size and on how far from shore it sails. The list for your boat is in its seaworthiness certificate: check the gear against it before each season and before a longer trip.

A safety harness clips you to the boat so you cannot go overboard in rough weather. Clip on before you leave the cockpit, to strong points or to jacklines: strong lines or webbing that run from bow to stern along both side decks. Keep the tether short, and clip on to the windward side (the side the wind comes from) when you can, so a fall throws you onto the deck rather than over the side.

Each type of flare has its own job, so carry the right mix:
• Red parachute rocket: climbs about 300 m and burns for about 40 seconds, so ships far away see it, by day or night.
• Red hand flare: shows your exact position to someone nearby, and keeps burning even if dropped in the water.
• Orange smoke: works by day only, and also shows a helicopter which way the wind blows.
Replace flares before their expiry date and store them dry and within reach. Hold a hand flare out over the downwind side, so the smoke and hot drips blow away from the boat.

Match the extinguisher to the fire, because the wrong one can make it worse:
• Foam: burning liquids such as fuel and oil. It covers the liquid and cuts it off from the air.
• Dry powder: most fires, including fuel and electrical ones.
• Carbon dioxide (CO2): electrical and engine-space fires.
• Fire blanket: a pan fire in the galley (the boat’s kitchen).
Never use water on burning fuel, which spreads it, or on live electrical equipment, which can give a shock. Know where each extinguisher is and check its pressure gauge and service date.

Refuelling is a fire risk, because fuel vapour is heavier than air and can collect inside the boat. Stop the engine, put out any flame and close the hatches. Switch off the automatic bilge pump (the pump that empties water from the bottom of the hull), so it cannot pump spilt fuel into the sea. Keep rags ready, check that the tank’s air vent is clear, and watch the gauge so the tank does not overflow.
observe: Find your boat’s seaworthiness certificate and check the listed safety gear against what is aboard.
Read the instructions printed on each flare and find its expiry date.
sail-58.mistake: Carrying expired flares or the wrong extinguisher, or clipping a harness to a weak fitting such as a guardrail.

quiz.prompt: What is a safety harness for?
options: Keeping the crew from going overboard in rough weather
quiz.explanation: Clipped to strong points or jacklines, the harness keeps you attached to the boat.

quiz.prompt: When can you use a red parachute rocket?
quiz.explanation: It climbs high and burns brightly, so it can be seen far away at any time of day.

quiz.prompt: Which fire is foam mainly for?
options: Burning liquids such as fuel and oil
quiz.explanation: Foam blankets a burning liquid and cuts it off from the air. Use powder or CO2 on electrical fires.

sail-58.transfer: Learn your own boat’s equipment with an instructor: fit the harness, read the flare instructions, find the extinguishers and attend a sea-survival course with a real life raft.
localNotes: The Israeli boat operator licence material expects, for example, a life raft on a private yacht sailing 15 NM from shore, at least 4 red parachute rockets, and a fire blanket where there is open-flame cooking. Your boat’s seaworthiness certificate gives the exact list; check the current Israeli regulations.

Under Israeli rules a boat is a vessel 7 to 24 m long. On a national voyage, along the Israeli coast, it may sail up to 12 NM from shore. A private boat’s seaworthiness is inspected every 24 months. The required equipment, including the anchor weight for the boat’s size, is set by the Israel Shipping and Ports Authority safety equipment regulations, published by the Authority and on the Ministry of Transport website.

sail-59.title: Life raft and abandoning ship
concepts:
Abandon the boat only when staying aboard is clearly more dangerous, for example when it is sinking or burning out of control. A boat that is still afloat is safer and easier to find than a raft. Before you go:
• Send a distress call.
• Put on lifejackets and warm clothing.
• Take the grab bag: water, a handheld VHF radio, an emergency beacon, flares and seasickness tablets.
Step up into the raft from the boat if you can, rather than jumping into the water, so you stay dry and warm.

Stow the life raft on deck or on the stern rail in its cradle, ready to launch quickly. Its painter, the line that ties it to the boat, is made fast to a strong point. A hydrostatic release frees the raft automatically if the boat sinks: at a depth of a few metres it lets go, the raft floats up and the painter pulls it open.

To launch, first check that the painter is tied to the boat. Throw the raft over the leeward side (the side away from the wind, where the boat shelters it) and pull out the painter. Its full length, printed on the canister, ends in a pull that fires the gas bottle and inflates the raft. When the raft is full, its relief valves whistle as the extra gas escapes. Keep it tied alongside while the crew boards.

If the raft inflates upside down, one swimmer can turn it over. Climb onto the gas bottle on its bottom, take hold of the righting strap and lean back, pulling the raft over. Do it from the downwind side, so the wind helps the raft flip toward you.

Once everyone is in, cut the painter with the raft’s safety knife and paddle clear of the sinking boat. Then:
• Stream the sea anchor, to stay near the position you reported and to steady the raft.
• Take seasickness tablets straight away, because vomiting loses body water.
• Close the canopy, bail out the water, keep warm and keep a lookout.
• Ration the water, and save flares for when you see a ship or aircraft.
The raft packs flares, a floating rescue line, a bailer, a repair kit and a survival manual. A radar transponder (SART), which shows up on a ship’s radar screen, is a separate item for the grab bag.

A sea anchor is a large cone or parachute streamed on a long line. From the bow of a boat or raft it holds the bow to the wind and waves and greatly reduces drift. In a survival storm with no sail left, it keeps a yacht from lying beam-on to the seas: side-on to the waves, which can roll her over. A drogue is smaller and towed astern. It slows a boat running down big waves, so she does not surf, swing sideways to a wave and broach (get knocked flat).
observe: Find where your boat’s life raft is stowed and read its canister: painter length, service date and hydrostatic release.
Check what is in the grab bag and who is responsible for taking it.
sail-59.mistake: Jumping into the water before the raft is ready, or forgetting to tie the painter before throwing the raft overboard.

quiz.prompt: What does a life raft’s hydrostatic release do?
options: Frees the raft automatically if the boat sinks
Keeps the raft locked until it is serviced
quiz.explanation: At a depth of a few metres it releases the raft so it floats up and inflates.

quiz.prompt: The raft has inflated upside down. How is it righted?
options: A swimmer stands on the gas bottle, holds the righting strap and leans back
Let the air out and inflate it again
It cannot be used; launch another raft
quiz.explanation: The righting strap on the bottom lets one person pull the raft upright, ideally from the downwind side.

quiz.prompt: Everyone is in the raft and clear of the boat. What do you do first?
options: Fire all the flares to reassure the crew
quiz.explanation: Seasickness quickly dehydrates people in a raft. Save flares for when a ship or aircraft is in sight.

sail-59.transfer: Learn your own boat’s equipment with an instructor: fit the harness, read the flare instructions, find the extinguishers and attend a sea-survival course with a real life raft.

sail-02.title: Know your yacht
concepts: Bow means the front; stern means the back. Port is the left side and starboard the right when facing the bow. These names stay with the boat however you face, so “rock to port” means the same side to everyone aboard.

The mainsail is behind the mast; the headsail is forward. The boom is the pole along the mainsail’s foot (bottom edge). The keel, the heavy fin underneath, helps keep the boat upright and resists the wind pushing it sideways; the rudder steers when water flows over it.
Use Chase for the whole boat, Helm for the sailing viewpoint, and Cockpit to inspect the wheel, winches, and screens.
observe: Switch to Cockpit and locate the wheel, the companionway (the steps down into the cabin), and the winches for pulling ropes.
Switch to Chase and identify the bow, mast, boom, and two sails.
sail-02.mistake: Calling a side port or starboard from whichever direction you happen to be looking.

quiz.prompt: You are facing the stern. Which side is port?
options: Whichever side the wind comes from
quiz.explanation: Port is the yacht’s left when facing forward, so it is on your right when facing aft.

quiz.prompt: What needs water flowing over it to steer effectively?
quiz.explanation: The rudder changes the direction of water flow. With little boat speed its authority is reduced.

sail-02.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-03.title: Lines, winches, and loads
concepts: A halyard raises a sail, and a sheet sets the sail's angle to the wind. A reef reduces the sail area you show. A cleat (a horn-shaped fitting) or a clutch (a lever lock) holds a line. A winch (a drum turned with a handle) takes the load, because a loaded sheet pulls harder than hands can hold.

On this yacht, the colored sheets run aft (toward the back) to the cockpit winches. Look at the wraps and clutches in Cockpit view. The Boat systems panel sets each of the two halyards and sheets separately, along with other controls explained on the next pages. In the app, the sliders set the controls; they do not show how you handle a real line.

The hoist controls set how far the mainsail and the headsail (the front sail) are raised. Each sheet sets one sail's angle, separately from the other. Three more controls shape the mainsail. The traveler slides the mainsheet's lower end across the boat. The vang pulls the boom (the pole under the sail) down, so the sail's top does not twist open. The outhaul stretches the bottom edge, which flattens the sail. Change one control at a time to see what each does.

The reef control makes the mainsail smaller, and the engine control sets reverse, neutral or ahead. Return to neutral before a sailing test, so only the sails drive the boat. The anchor rode (the rope or chain to the anchor) slider sets a target. The windlass (the motor winch at the front) lets the rode out or pulls it in over time; watch how much is actually out, and stop it when needed.

Keep fingers, loose clothing and hair away from loaded lines, because they can be pulled into a winch. Learn real winch work, line handling and knots with an instructor, including how to ease a loaded line under control. In the app, a mouse cannot teach you the feel of a loaded line.

The vang, or kicking strap, keeps the boom down so the top of the sail keeps its power. On a reach (wind from the side) or a run (wind from behind), the mainsheet pulls the boom out more than down. Without the vang, the boom rises and the top of the sail twists open and loses power. In a strong gust, easing the vang lets the top of the sail spill wind.
observe: Follow a colored sheet from the deck to its winch.
Compare a halyard's job (lifting the sail) with a sheet's job (setting its angle).
sail-03.mistake: Treating a heavily loaded sheet like a slack rope, or mixing up the sheet and the halyard.

quiz.prompt: You want to change the mainsail's angle. Which line does that?
quiz.explanation: The mainsheet controls the boom and so the mainsail's angle; the halyard raises the sail.

quiz.prompt: Can the app's winch model teach you to handle a loaded rope safely?
options: No; handling real lines needs supervised practice
quiz.explanation: The drawn hardware shows you where things are. It does not simulate hand position, friction or line loads.

sail-03.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-60.title: Ropes, wire, knots and pulleys
concepts: Ropes are made from different fibres, and each suits a different job. Nylon stretches a lot, so it absorbs shocks: use it for anchor and mooring lines. Polyester stretches little, so the sail keeps its shape: use it for sheets and halyards. Polypropylene floats, which suits a rescue throwing line, but it chafes and weakens in sunlight. Aramid and similar fibres, such as Kevlar and Dyneema, are the strongest for their size and hardly stretch.

A mooring or tow line needs a high breaking strength, and a tow line must also be long and able to stretch. One strong line is better than two weak ones, because a load rarely shares evenly between two lines. Every knot or splice weakens a rope: a knot can take away up to about half its strength, a splice much less. Chafe weakens it too, so protect lines where they pass through fairleads.

Look after your ropes, because sunlight and salt crystals weaken the fibres. Rinse the salt out with fresh water, dry them and store them coiled in the shade. Check for chafe, cuts and stiff or glazed patches, and replace a rope before it fails.

Wire rope is described by its strands and wires. A marking such as 6/12 means 6 strands with 12 wires in each. 7×19 wire, 7 strands of 19 wires, is flexible and suits running rigging (the lines you adjust) that bends round sheaves (pulley wheels). 1×19 wire, a single strand of 19 wires, is stiff and stretches little, so it suits standing rigging (the fixed wires holding up the mast), such as the shrouds at its sides, and guardrails.

One more line you will meet is the topping lift, from the masthead (the top of the mast) to the end of the boom. It holds the boom up when the mainsail is lowered or reefed, so the boom does not drop into the cockpit or onto the crew.

A block and tackle multiplies your pull; the mainsheet on the boom is one. A block is a pulley: one is fixed to the boat, the other moves with the load. Count the rope parts that hold up the moving block: with four parts, a 320 kg load needs about 80 kg of pull, ignoring friction. With two double blocks (two wheels each), if the rope leaves from the moving block there are five parts, a gain of 5 to 1; if it leaves from the fixed block, 4 to 1. You pull that much more rope for the same lift.

Know a few knots well enough to tie them in the dark:
• Bowline: makes a loop that will not slip or jam.
• Cleat hitch: makes a line fast to a cleat.
• Clove hitch: quickly holds a fender on a rail.
• Figure-of-eight: stops a line running out through a block.
• Round turn and two half hitches: ties a line to a ring or post under load.
observe: Find the anchor line, a sheet and a halyard aboard and say which fibre each is made of, and why.
Count the parts of rope at the moving block of the mainsheet tackle and work out its gain.
sail-60.mistake: Joining two weak lines in place of one strong one, or forgetting that a knot weakens the rope it is tied in.

quiz.prompt: Which rope is the strongest for its thickness?
quiz.explanation: Aramid fibres such as Kevlar are far stronger than nylon or polypropylene of the same size.

quiz.prompt: What does a knot do to a rope’s strength?
quiz.explanation: Every knot or splice weakens a rope; a knot can take away up to about half its strength.

quiz.prompt: Two double blocks, with the rope leaving from the moving block. What is the gain?
quiz.explanation: Count the parts at the moving block: four between the blocks plus the one leaving it make five.

sail-60.transfer: Practise the knots with a real rope until you can tie them without looking, and ask an instructor to check how lines are led and protected aboard your boat.

sail-04.title: Read the instruments
concepts: Heading is the direction the bow points, measured clockwise from north: 000° north, 090° east, 180° south, 270° west. Speed is shown in knots; one knot is one nautical mile per hour.

The multifunction display behind the wheel and the dashboard below the controls show the same live readings. Wind over water is the wind measured against the water rather than the land (Lesson {lesson:sail-05} explains it); its angle is measured from the bow. Depth estimates water depth, not clearance below the keel: subtract the keel’s depth, or you can run aground in water that looks deep enough.

Current and leeway (sideways slip from the wind) can push you off your heading. Course and speed over ground, from GPS, are your real track and speed over the seabed. Compare them with heading and speed through water on the dashboard. You can enlarge the display for easier reading.

The app combines a compass and a wind indicator in one dial. North stays at the top, east at the right, south at the bottom, and west at the left, even when the boat or camera turns. Read the white boat symbol’s bow against the compass scale to find your heading.

The gold arrow identifies where wind over water comes from. The shaded no-go sector surrounds that source; it marks headings too close to the wind for sailing (explained in Lesson {lesson:sail-05}). In this example, the white boat points northeast at 045°, while the arrow and sector face northwest at 315°. The knots reading beneath the dial is wind speed.
observe: Open Helm or Cockpit and compare the multifunction display behind the wheel with the dashboard below the controls.
Select Chart and find the yacht symbol and north arrow.
Find the floating compass. Identify north, read the white boat’s heading, then read the gold wind-from arrow. These are two separate bearings.
sail-04.mistake: Reading depth as guaranteed clearance or treating heading as a guaranteed ground track.

quiz.prompt: Which heading points east?
quiz.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from north; east is 090°.

quiz.prompt: At 6 knots, how far would you travel in 30 minutes without current?
quiz.explanation: Distance = speed × time. Six nautical miles per hour for half an hour is three nautical miles.

quiz.prompt: On the illustrated app compass, the white bow points to 045° and the gold arrow to 315°. What is your heading?
quiz.explanation: Heading comes from the white boat’s bow: 045°. The gold arrow gives the wind-from bearing, 315°. Neither the wind pointer nor the shaded sector is a course to follow.

sail-04.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Inspect the cockpit instruments
Open the navigation chart

practice.debrief: You can now locate the displays. Check instruments regularly while maintaining an outside lookout.

sail-05.title: Where the wind comes from
concepts: Wind is named for where it comes from. A northwesterly wind comes from the northwest (315°) and blows toward the southeast (135°). Windward is the side the wind comes from; leeward is the side it blows toward. Sailors name the source because that is where the wind’s force, the waves and any approaching weather come from.

A sail is a flexible wing: it only works when air flows across it at an angle. Point the bow straight into the wind and the sail lines up with the airflow and just flaps like a flag, so it makes no driving force. The no-go zone is the range of headings too close to the wind for the sail to work: about 40–45° on either side for most cruising yachts (on a clock face, from 12 round to between the 1 and the 2), and 38° in this simulator. To reach a place upwind, you sail a zigzag outside it.

The wind you sail by is the wind over the water. If the water itself is moving (a current), that wind differs from the forecast, which gives the wind over a fixed point: a current flowing with the wind makes the wind you feel weaker. Once the boat moves, it also feels its own airflow, called apparent wind (Lesson {lesson:sail-17}). With no current, the forecast wind is the one that matters.

The app’s compass shows the wind like a weather vane: the gold arrowhead points to where the wind comes from. The shaded no-go sector sits around it. Diagrams of moving air point the other way, toward where the air goes. In the example, wind from 315° and a heading of 045° are 90° apart: a beam reach, with the wind straight across the side (Lesson {lesson:sail-09}). When the boat turns, only the white boat symbol moves; the gold arrow and the sector stay where the wind is.
observe: With no current and wind from 315°, compare headings 315°, 045°, and 135° on the compass.
The 045° heading puts the wind approximately across the side.
On the app compass, compare the white bow with the shaded sector. Say where the wind comes from and where the air moves before choosing a heading.
sail-05.mistake: Interpreting the arrow as where the wind is going rather than where it comes from.

quiz.prompt: A wind from 315° comes from which direction?
quiz.explanation: 315° is northwest. Wind direction is conventionally named for its source.

quiz.prompt: Why can a yacht not sail straight into the wind?
options: The sail lines up with the airflow and just flaps, so it makes no driving force
quiz.explanation: A sail needs air flowing across it at an angle. Outside the no-go zone it works like a wing; to go upwind you zigzag by tacking, turning the bow through the wind from one zigzag to the next.

quiz.prompt: Why do the app’s gold arrow and shaded no-go sector both face 315° in this example?
options: They tell you to steer toward 315°
Both identify the wind’s source; the air moves toward 135°
quiz.explanation: The pointer marks wind from 315°, and the sector marks headings too close to that source. Air flows toward 135°. The white boat at 045° is outside the sector, on a beam reach.

sail-05.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-06.title: Raise the sails
concepts: Hoist the mainsail with the bow pointing into the wind. The sail then lines up with the airflow and flaps with almost no load (it luffs), so it slides up easily and the boom cannot swing hard. With the sheet eased, the sail cannot fill by surprise.

Before hoisting, check the lines, the space and the crew. Halyards and sheets must be clear and not twisted, because a twisted line jams the sail half-way up. Make sure you have room to drift while you work. Keep the crew clear of the boom, which can swing. The mainsail usually goes up first: it sits at the back of the boat, so like the tail of a weather vane it helps hold the bow toward the wind while you work. The headsail follows. In the app, Raise sails hoists both at once; Boat systems hoists each one separately.

A raised sail facing the wind still makes no drive. To get moving, bear away (turn the bow away from the wind) until the wind is well to one side, then sheet in (pull the sheets in) until the sails stop flapping. Only then do they work as wings.

Sails are also your backup engine, so keep one ready to set when motoring near a harbor. If the engine stops between the breakwaters (the harbor walls), unroll or hoist a sail at once so the boat keeps drive and steering and you can sail clear. Anchoring in the entrance blocks it, and the anchor may not hold before the boat reaches the rocks.
observe: Start the exercise facing into the wind with sails lowered.
Raise the sails; then turn to a sailable course in later exercises.
sail-06.mistake: Assuming raised sails always propel the boat, or hoisting without first checking the lines and boom area.

quiz.prompt: Before a real mainsail hoist, what should be checked?
options: Clear lines, sea room, crew, and an unloaded sail
Whether the boat is at top speed
quiz.explanation: Preparation prevents jams and unexpected sail loading.

quiz.prompt: Why is the mainsail hoisted with the bow pointing into the wind?
options: The sail flaps with almost no load, so it goes up easily and the boom stays quiet
It makes the boat go fastest
quiz.explanation: Pointing into the wind, the sail lines up with the airflow and carries little load. Across the wind it would fill, pull hard and swing the boom while you are still hoisting.

sail-06.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

practice.debrief: You set the sails in the model. The next exercise starts on a reach where they can produce drive.

sail-07.title: Feel the boat accelerate
concepts: A beam reach puts the wind at about 90° to the boat. It is the easiest point of sail to start on: you are far from the no-go zone, and the sail can be set at a clear angle to the wind, so it makes plenty of forward drive.

A yacht weighs several tonnes, so it speeds up slowly. Water drag also grows quickly with speed. The boat accelerates until the push from the sails equals the drag from the water, then settles at a steady speed. Change the wind or the trim and it finds a new balance, again gradually.

The rudder is a small underwater wing that only steers when water flows past it. So it does little at rest and grips better as speed builds; use small helm movements. Which way the bow turns:
• Wheel: steers like a car; turn it to port and the bow goes to port.
• Tiller: works the opposite way; push it to starboard to turn the bow to port.
• Going backward: water reaches the rudder from behind, so the same helm turns the bow the other way.

Waves change how well the rudder grips, too: steering works best when the boat heads into them. Then water flows quickly past the rudder and the bow meets each wave. Running with the waves, especially fast, each wave lifts the stern and the flow past the rudder drops, so the boat can swing off course. Steer actively, and slow down if the course becomes hard to hold.
observe: Begin on 045° with a northwesterly wind, sails lowered, and anchor up.
Raise both sails, then watch speed increase. Keep the helm centered while the yacht builds enough speed to steer.
sail-07.mistake: Applying full helm while stationary and expecting the yacht to pivot instantly.

quiz.prompt: When does this rudder gain steering authority?
options: As water flow and boat speed increase
quiz.explanation: A yacht normally needs water flow over the rudder to respond.

quiz.prompt: After centering the helm, what happens?
options: The yacht returns automatically to north
The turn reduces and the yacht tends to maintain its new heading
quiz.explanation: The helm controls turning, not a selected compass heading.

sail-07.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Raise sails and build speed above 3 knots

practice.debrief: The sail force accelerated the boat; the rudder became useful as speed built.

sail-08.title: Hold a steady course
concepts: Steer by something far away, such as a headland or a cloud, and use the compass to check it. A distant mark shows a turn at once; the compass number lags behind and swings in waves.

A turning boat keeps turning after you center the helm, because it carries turning momentum, like a revolving door. So center the helm before you reach the new heading and let the boat glide onto it. If you wait until you are on the heading, you overshoot, correct back and zigzag. Small, early corrections give a straight track.

If you keep needing helm just to hold a straight course, the boat is telling you something. A yacht that keeps trying to turn toward the wind (weather helm) usually has too much sail up or is heeling too far; easing the mainsheet (letting it out) or reefing (making the sail smaller) fixes it (Lesson {lesson:sail-18}). Keep a lookout too, because a well-steered course can still lead into danger.
observe: Use short port or starboard inputs, then select Center.
Watch heading settle rather than keeping the helm over.
sail-08.mistake: Holding a large correction too long and oscillating from one side of the target to the other.

quiz.prompt: You are approaching your intended heading. What usually helps avoid overshoot?
options: Center the helm in good time
quiz.explanation: The boat keeps turning for a moment, like a revolving door, so reducing the correction early helps the turn settle.

quiz.prompt: Which is a complete steering routine?
options: Look away until the boat drifts
Look out, check heading, make a small correction, reassess
quiz.explanation: Steering and lookout must happen together.

sail-08.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold 045° ±5°, above 2 knots, for 10 seconds
steps.hint: Port brings 060° down toward 045°. Center before you reach the target.

practice.debrief: A steady course requires small corrections and anticipation, not continuous large helm input.

sail-09.title: Find a beam reach
concepts:
A point of sail is the angle between the bow and the wind, not a compass heading. Moving away from the wind:
• Close hauled: about 40–50° off the wind, sails pulled in tight.
• Close reach: about 60°.
• Beam reach: 90°, wind straight across the side.
• Broad reach: about 135°, wind from behind the side.
• Run: about 180°, wind from straight behind.

Each point of sail has its own sail setting. A rough guide is that the sail sits at about half the wind angle: close hauled the boom is near the centerline, on a beam reach it is about halfway out, and on a run it is far out. You can be on any point of sail with the wind on either side: with wind from 315°, both 045° and 225° are beam reaches, one with the wind on the port side and one on starboard.

As the boat speeds up, the wind it feels swings forward, because its own motion adds a breeze from ahead (Lesson {lesson:sail-17} explains this). So trim in a little as you accelerate. If the wind shifts, your point of sail changes even when your heading does not.

Running before the wind, or simply running, means sailing with the wind and the waves coming from behind. It feels calm because the apparent wind is small and the boat barely heels. But the waves lift the stern, and the risk of an accidental gybe, the boom swinging across without warning, is highest.
observe: Compare the bow marker with the direction of wind over water on the onboard display.
Notice that two different compass headings can give the same point of sail.
sail-09.mistake: Memorizing a compass heading as a point of sail when the wind direction may change.

quiz.prompt: What defines a beam reach?
quiz.explanation: Points of sail are relative to the wind.

quiz.prompt: If the wind shifts, can an unchanged heading produce a different point of sail?
quiz.explanation: A wind shift changes the angle between the bow and the wind.

sail-09.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold a beam reach above 2 knots for 8 seconds

practice.debrief: You selected a course using the wind relationship, rather than the compass alone.

sail-10.title: Sail close hauled
concepts: How can a boat sail toward the wind? Air flowing around the curved sail makes a force, like the lift on an aircraft wing. Close hauled, that force points mostly sideways and only a little forward. The keel grips the water and resists the sideways part, so what is left drives the boat forward. That is why close hauled feels heeled (leaning over) and slower than a reach, and why the boat slides sideways a little (leeway).

Pointing as close to the wind as you can is not always fastest upwind. Steer too close to the wind (pinching) and the front of the sail starts to flap, drive drops and the boat slows; a slower keel grips less, so the boat also slips sideways more. A few degrees lower with good speed usually gets you upwind sooner. As you head up (turn toward the wind), trim in; if speed fades, bear away (turn away from it) a little.

Telltales are short ribbons on both sides of the sail near its front edge. When both stream straight back, the air is flowing well. If one misbehaves:
• Windward one (on the side the wind comes from) lifts or spins: you are too close to the wind or the sail is too far out. Bear away a little or trim in.
• Leeward one droops or spins: the sail is pulled in too far. Ease it or head up a little.
observe: Start on a reach and steer nearer to the wind.
Trim inward as the wind angle decreases.
sail-10.mistake: Pinching: pointing too close to the wind and losing the speed that makes the boat and rudder work.

quiz.prompt: What is pinching?
options: Sailing too close to the wind and losing useful drive
Sailing with too much anchor chain
quiz.explanation: A slightly lower course may produce better upwind progress because it preserves speed.

quiz.prompt: Relative to a beam reach, a close-hauled mainsail is generally…
quiz.explanation: As you sail closer to the wind, the sail angle normally comes inward.

sail-10.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold 45°–58° off the wind above 2 knots

practice.debrief: You balanced pointing with boat speed. The simulator estimates leeway but does not assess reading physical telltales.

sail-11.title: Bear away to a broad reach
concepts: Bearing away turns the bow away from the wind and makes the wind angle larger. Ease the sheets as you turn, so each sail keeps its angle to the wind. If you leave them tight, the sail stalls: it heels the boat and pushes it sideways without making much speed.

As you turn downwind, the sail works less like a wing and more like a parachute: the wind mostly pushes on it from behind. The sideways force fades, so the boat heels less and feels calmer. On a broad reach, with the wind from behind the side, many boats are fast and comfortable.

Near dead downwind, watch the boom, because it can suddenly swing across. If the wind comes round to the boom’s side (sailing by the lee), it can cause an accidental gybe: the stern swings through the wind and the boom slams across, hitting heads and breaking gear. While learning, keep the wind over the back corner, about 150° off the wind or less, and know which side the boom would swing to.

When someone must work on the foredeck (the deck at the front) in strong wind and big waves, bear away to a broad reach. The boat heels less, the bow slams less and the apparent wind drops because you are moving with the wind, while you stay clear of the dead run where an accidental gybe is likely. Hold a steady course until the crew is back.
observe: Increase your angle to the wind, then ease the sheet.
Keep a margin from dead downwind while learning.
sail-11.mistake: Leaving the mainsheet tight after bearing away or losing track of which side the boom will move to.

quiz.prompt: What happens to wind angle when you bear away?
quiz.explanation: The bow moves farther away from the source of the wind.

quiz.prompt: What maneuver becomes a concern near dead downwind?
quiz.explanation: A small heading or wind change can take the wind across the stern and move the boom.

sail-11.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold a broad reach, 120°–150° off the wind

practice.debrief: You increased the wind angle and kept clear of an accidental stern crossing.

sail-12.title: Trim with feedback
concepts: Trim means setting the sail at the right angle to the wind. Too far out and the front edge flaps (luffing): air is not flowing across the sail properly, so it makes little drive. Too far in and the air breaks away from the back of the sail (stalling), like a wing tipped too steeply: the boat heels and slows but does not speed up. The best setting is just inside the point where luffing starts.

The classic method: ease the sheet slowly until the front of the sail starts to flap, then pull it in just until the flapping stops. Telltales make this easier to see. Repeat it after every course change or wind shift. “When in doubt, let it out”: a slightly eased sail costs little speed; an over-tight one costs a lot.

Change one thing at a time and give the boat time. Speed changes slowly (Lesson {lesson:sail-07}), so wait several seconds to see whether a change helped. In this app, the “Suggested” value under the Mainsheet slider, worked out from the apparent wind (the wind the moving boat feels), lets you check your result; on a real boat you trim by watching the sail’s front edge and the telltales.
observe: Leave the helm centered and change only the sheet.
Wait for speed to respond instead of making constant large changes.
sail-12.mistake: Changing heading and sheet simultaneously so you cannot tell which adjustment improved the boat.

quiz.prompt: For a useful trim comparison, which technique helps?
options: Hold a steady course and adjust one thing at a time
quiz.explanation: A stable course makes the effects of sheet changes easier to observe.

quiz.prompt: Both telltales are streaming. You pull the sheet in further and the leeward telltale starts to spin. What happened?
options: The sail is pulled in too far and starting to stall
quiz.explanation: Pulling in too far makes the airflow break away on the back (leeward) side. Ease the sheet until the leeward telltale streams again.

sail-12.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold efficient trim and speed for 10 seconds

practice.debrief: You used a controlled adjustment and allowed time for the speed response.

sail-13.title: Head up and bear away
concepts: Heading up means turning toward the wind; bearing away means turning away from it. Port (left) and starboard (right) only say which way the boat turns. "Turn left" tells you nothing about the wind, so you must know which side the wind is on.

Whether a left turn heads up depends on your tack (which side the wind comes over). With the wind from the north, heading east, turning left heads up; heading west, the same left turn bears away. So check the wind first, then trim to match: head up and pull the sheets (the sail ropes) in; bear away and let them out.

Practice both turns: sail first at 50° off the wind, then at 110°. At 110° the wind is a little behind the beam (straight out to the side). Let each course settle before the next change, so you can see what the turn did.
observe: Notice whether the wind angle grows or shrinks with each helm input.
Center the helm at each target, and adjust trim to the new point of sail.

quiz.prompt: Is a port (left) turn always a turn toward the wind?
options: No; it depends on the tack and wind direction
quiz.explanation: The same helm movement changes your angle to the wind in opposite ways on opposite tacks.

quiz.prompt: What should you do after a big course change?
options: Check sail trim and lookout again
quiz.explanation: The new heading changes the airflow on the sails and what is around the boat.

sail-13.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Settle at 45°–55° off the wind
Bear away and settle at 105°–115°

practice.debrief: You changed your relationship to the wind in both directions and stabilized between turns.

sail-14.title: Make a controlled tack
concepts: A tack turns the bow through the wind, so the wind moves to the other side of the boat and the sails swap sides. From close hauled to close hauled, it is a turn of about 90°. Before you start, look for traffic, check sea room (open water with no boats or shore to hit while you turn) and warn the crew with “Ready about”.

Speed is what gets you through. Inside the no-go zone the sails flap and make no drive, so only the boat’s momentum carries the bow across. Start with good speed and turn steadily. Too slow, and the boat stops head to wind (in irons, Lesson {lesson:sail-16}). Too sharp, and the rudder, turned hard over, acts as a brake.

On a real yacht, each step of the tack has its own moment:
• Put the helm over and call the turn, for example “Lee-ho”, meaning the turn starts now.
• As the headsail starts to flap, release its old sheet.
• As the bow passes the wind, pull in the new sheet on the other side.
• Center the helm on the new close-hauled course and retrim.
Expect to lose some speed, and rebuild it before pointing high. In the app the sails swap sides automatically.
observe: Start with wind over the starboard side, then turn to starboard so the bow swings past 315°, where the wind comes from.
Continue past the no-go zone, center the helm, and rebuild speed.
sail-14.mistake: Stopping the turn in the no-go zone, or calling a turn across the stern a tack.

quiz.prompt: Which part of the yacht crosses the wind during a tack?
quiz.explanation: A tack takes the bow through the source of the wind; a gybe takes the stern through it.

quiz.prompt: Before the turn, what is needed?
options: Lookout, sea room, preparation, and enough boat speed
All crew standing beneath the boom
quiz.explanation: Preparation and momentum help the boat complete the no-go-zone crossing.

sail-14.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Turn the bow through the wind and recover above 2 knots
steps.hint: Turn starboard through 315°, then continue to about 005° and center. Trim for the new course.

practice.debrief: The assessment recorded a bow crossing, a new tack, and recovered speed. Sheet transfer remains an on-water skill.

sail-15.title: Make a planned gybe
concepts: A gybe turns the stern through the wind. It is more dangerous than a tack because the sails stay full the whole time. In a tack the sails go slack as the bow passes the wind; in a gybe the wind gets behind the mainsail and throws the boom across the cockpit with force.

So you control the boom and warn the crew (“Stand by to gybe”) to keep heads clear. Before the stern crosses the wind, pull the mainsheet in so the boom is near the center and has only a short distance to swing. Turn slowly. As the boom crosses, ease the sheet out smoothly on the new side. Then steady the helm, because the boat tends to swing up into the wind.

Make it a small, deliberate turn from a broad reach on one side to a broad reach on the other. An accidental gybe is the dangerous version because nobody is ready. It usually comes from sailing by the lee (the wind coming over the same side the boom is on), when the boom can flip across without warning. In the app the boom is animated, but its impact force is not modeled.

In strong wind a gybe can break gear or injure the crew. If you need to turn from one broad reach to the other, consider going the long way round: head up, tack through the wind, then bear away on the new side. It takes longer, but the boom never swings across with full force.
observe: Start at 160° with wind from 315°, so the wind is behind you on a broad reach. Turn port toward and through 135°.
Settle near 110° and keep the wind well aft of the beam.
sail-15.mistake: Treating a gybe like an unannounced sharp turn with the mainsheet fully loose.

quiz.prompt: What is the principal gybe hazard for the crew?
options: The boom and mainsheet crossing the cockpit
quiz.explanation: Control the boom and keep people clear of its path.

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes a gybe from a tack?
options: The stern passes through the wind
The boat must use an engine
quiz.explanation: The wind crosses the stern during a gybe and the bow during a tack.

sail-15.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Cross the wind with the stern and settle on the new tack
steps.hint: Turn port through 135° and settle near 110°. Center the helm.

practice.debrief: You made the correct stern crossing. Real mainsheet control must be learned with supervision.

sail-16.title: Recover from loss of drive
concepts: In irons means stopped, or nearly stopped, pointing into the wind. The sails flap, so there is no drive, and as speed falls the rudder loses its grip on the water.

Avoid it by keeping speed through a tack and not pinching (steering so close to the wind that the sails lose power). If you notice it early, use the speed you still have: bear away promptly until the sails fill, then trim to rebuild drive.

A fully stopped boat needs another way to turn. On a real yacht the crew can hold the headsail out on one side (backing it) so the wind pushes the bow away, or let the boat drift backward and steer it round, remembering that steering works the opposite way going backward. Some crews use the engine. Backing sails is not modeled here, so this exercise starts with some speed left: use it before it runs out.
observe: Use the speed you still have to turn away from 315°, the direction the wind comes from.
Do not wait until speed reaches zero before correcting.
sail-16.mistake: Expecting the rudder to rotate a fully stationary yacht without water flow.

quiz.prompt: Why should you act before all speed is lost?
options: Residual water flow gives steering authority
quiz.explanation: Water still flowing past the rudder lets you steer, so use it to get outside the no-go zone.

quiz.prompt: The boat has stopped head to wind and starts to drift backward. What happens to the steering?
options: It works the opposite way: the same helm turns the bow the other way
It works exactly as when moving forward
quiz.explanation: Moving backward, water reaches the rudder from behind, so its effect reverses. Crews use this, together with a backed headsail, to turn the bow out of the no-go zone.

sail-16.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Exit the no-go zone and rebuild speed above 2 knots
steps.hint: Turn starboard toward 010° or beyond before the remaining way disappears.

practice.debrief: You used residual momentum. A stopped-boat recovery is a separate practical skill.

sail-17.title: True and apparent wind
concepts: On a moving boat you feel the apparent wind, like the headwind you feel cycling in still air. It is the true wind plus the breeze of your own motion. True wind is what you would feel standing still. Instruments measure it over the ground or over the water (these differ in a current), so check which yours shows.

As the boat speeds up on a reach (wind from the side), the apparent wind usually moves forward, toward the bow (the front). That is because your own breeze comes from straight ahead. Sailing downwind, you move with the air, so the apparent wind can get weaker. With no wind over the water, there is no wind direction, but a moving yacht still feels the breeze of its own motion.

Name your course from the wind over water, but trim the sails to the apparent wind. In the app, compare Wind over water with Apparent wind on the onboard display. The point of sail (your angle to the wind) and the no-go zone (too close to the wind to sail) come from the wind over water. Trim to the apparent wind, because that is the air the sails actually feel; telltales (ribbons on the sail) and sail shape always show it directly.

A sail works like an aircraft wing: it bends the airflow and pushes the boat partly forward and partly sideways. The keel (the fin under the hull), centreboard or underwater foils (small wings) resist the sideways push, so the forward part drives the boat. On a reach, a well-trimmed sail can keep driving even above true-wind speed. The boat stops speeding up when the forward push equals the water's resistance.

Some efficient racing boats can therefore sail faster than the true wind. Light hulls and efficient sails help. Hydrofoils can lift the hull clear of the water, which cuts resistance even more. All the energy still comes from the wind moving over the water. An ordinary cruising yacht may have too much resistance to beat the wind's speed.

In this example the apparent wind is stronger than the true wind and comes from further ahead. Assume no current and no leeway (sideways slip). A racing boat goes north at 30 knots (about 55 km/h) while a 20-knot wind blows from the west, at a right angle to its path. The apparent wind is about 36 knots, coming from about 34° to port (left) of the bow. Side note: because the two speeds are at right angles, they combine as √(20² + 30²) ≈ 36.1 knots. If the boat instead sailed straight downwind at the wind's speed, it would feel no wind at all in this simple case.

Try it in Challenges → Apparent Wind Lab: record the wind at three moments:
• With the sails down.
• On a beam reach (wind straight from the side).
• On a broad reach (wind from behind the side).
On the beam reach, the apparent wind gets stronger and moves forward as speed builds; on the broad reach it gets weaker.
observe: Imagine riding a bicycle in still air: you feel wind from ahead.
Compare the apparent wind display as speed increases on a steady course.
sail-17.mistake: Assuming true and apparent wind have the same direction and speed while the yacht is moving.

quiz.prompt: Which wind does a moving sail actually feel?
quiz.explanation: Sails work with the airflow as it meets the moving yacht.

quiz.prompt: You speed up on a steady beam reach. What happens to the apparent wind?
options: It moves forward and gets stronger
It moves aft and gets weaker
quiz.explanation: The boat’s own motion adds a breeze from ahead. Combined with the true wind, the apparent wind swings toward the bow and strengthens, so you trim in a little.

quiz.prompt: Why can an efficient racing boat sail faster than the true wind on a reach?
options: Boat motion creates an unlimited energy supply
The sail's lift can still push forward harder than the water resists
Every sailboat automatically matches apparent wind speed
quiz.explanation: The sail feels the apparent wind, while the keel and other underwater parts resist the sideways push. If resistance is low enough, the forward push can stay bigger than resistance even above true-wind speed. The energy still comes from the wind over the water.

quiz.prompt: With no current or leeway, a boat goes 30 knots at a right angle to a 20-knot true wind. What apparent wind speed does it feel?
quiz.explanation: Speeds at right angles combine as √(20² + 30²) ≈ 36.1 knots. You only add or subtract speeds directly when they point along the same line. The example assumes the boat already does 30 knots.

sail-17.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-18.title: Reef before you need to
concepts: A reef makes the mainsail smaller and lower, and it pays to do it early. Wind force grows with the square of wind speed: 20 knots pushes about four times as hard as 10 knots, not twice. So a moderate rise in wind makes a big rise in the force heeling the boat and loading the rig. A smaller, lower sail catches less of that force and holds it lower down, which means less heel.

Too much heel does not make a boat faster. The hull slips sideways more, the rudder grips less, and the boat keeps trying to turn into the wind (weather helm). Signs that it is time to reef: heavy steering, the boat rounding up toward the wind in gusts, and water along the side deck. “Reef when you first think about it”: it is far easier before the wind builds than during it.

There is no single wind speed for reefing: it depends on the boat, the crew, the gusts and the sea. Compare the heel and the helm before and after a reef on the same course. The app’s Reef control shortens the main in one step; on a real boat it means handling the halyard (the rope that raises and lowers the sail) and the reefing lines (which pull the lower part down) under load, with the crew working together.

Which sail you shrink also changes the steering. Sails behind the boat’s pivot point (the spot the boat turns around), such as the mainsail, turn the bow toward the wind; the headsail, in front, turns it away. Lower the headsail and the boat heads up; sail on the headsail alone and it bears away. On a boat with two masts, such as a ketch, the aft sail, called the mizzen, adds weather helm: when the helm gets heavy or the wind rises, reduce or lower the mizzen first, then reef the main.

In a storm, reduce sail but do not take it all down. A small, well-set sail keeps the boat moving and steering and steadies the roll; a boat with no sail at all lies across the waves and cannot be steered.
observe: Observe heel and speed in the exercise’s 22-knot breeze.
Select Reef, keep the boat on a reach, and compare its response.
sail-18.mistake: Waiting until the crew are overloaded or using a fixed wind threshold without considering the boat.

quiz.prompt: What is a sound reason to reef early?
options: Increasing difficulty keeping the yacht controlled
Every yacht always reefs at exactly 20 knots
quiz.explanation: Reefing is a control decision based on boat, crew, and conditions.

quiz.prompt: The wind rises from 10 to 20 knots. Roughly how much harder does it push on the sails?
quiz.explanation: Wind force grows with the square of wind speed: 2 × 2 = 4. That is why reefing decisions come earlier than many beginners expect.

sail-18.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Set a reef and maintain steerage for 10 seconds

practice.debrief: You reduced sail area and retained control. Real reefing needs a practiced crew procedure.

sail-19.title: Reduce power deliberately
concepts: A sailing yacht has no brakes, so plan every stop early. When you take power out of the sails, the boat keeps moving on its momentum and slows only as water drag works on it. A heavy boat can glide a long way, so leave sea room.

Ways to take power out, from quickest to most complete:
• Ease the sheets until the sails flap, so they stop working as wings.
• Head up toward the wind, which reduces the angle and the drive.
• Lower the sails, which removes drive completely.
As the boat slows, the rudder grips less, so steering becomes slow and weak.
In this exercise, lower the sails and wait until the speed is below 1 knot. Do not use the anchor as a brake: dropping it at speed can rip out the gear, damage the boat or snag the bottom.

On a real yacht you can also heave to: set the sails to work against each other so the boat almost stops. Tack without releasing the headsail, so it stays held on the wrong (windward) side; this is the backed headsail. Then steer as if to head up (tiller pushed away from the wind) and ease the main. The backed headsail pushes the bow away from the wind while the main and rudder push it back. The boat lies about 60° off the true wind, between close hauled and a beam reach, and drifts slowly to leeward. Use it to rest, reef or wait in strong wind; the app does not model it.
observe: Compare the speed before and after lowering sails.
Notice the delay and the reduction in rudder authority.
sail-19.mistake: Dropping an anchor at speed as a routine way to stop.

quiz.prompt: What remains after you lower the sails?
quiz.explanation: The boat continues to move until drag reduces its speed.

quiz.prompt: Why leave room when slowing down?
options: Stopping distance and declining steerage need to be anticipated
The compass becomes unreliable at low speed
quiz.explanation: Plan your speed reduction early enough to remain in control.

sail-19.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Lower the sails
Coast below 1 knot without anchoring

practice.debrief: You allowed momentum to decay instead of expecting an immediate stop.

sail-20.title: Choose a weather limit
concepts:
Read a marine forecast for the whole trip and some time beyond it, because a change can come earlier or later than forecast and trips often run long. Check three groups:
• Wind: average strength, gusts and changes of direction.
• Water: sea state (the size of the waves), tides and currents.
• Other: visibility, temperature and local effects, such as a sea breeze or wind speeding up around a headland.

Three situations make a moderate wind more dangerous than it sounds:
• Wind against current: the current squeezes the waves together, so they get taller, steeper and closer, and can break.
• A lee shore, a coast the wind blows toward: if the engine, a sail or the rudder fails, the wind pushes you onto it.
• An offshore wind, blowing from the land: it feels calm near the coast, but the waves grow farther out and it can be hard to get back.

Set your go/no-go limits before you leave: the conditions in which you will not go, or will turn back. Decide too what change would make you shorten the trip, and where you would go instead. The simulator’s wind is steady and its current does not change, so practice this judgment here as planning; real weather changes.

When strong wind is forecast while you are in harbor, prepare the boat. Double the mooring lines and add fenders and chafe protection. Take the sails down and stow them below, or lash them tightly, and remove anything the wind can catch.

Forecasts and the barometer tell you when to wait or turn back:
• A low-pressure system moving toward your route brings strong wind and rising seas. Wait until it has passed rather than trying to beat it.
• A falling barometer warns that the weather is getting worse.
• If the forecast worsens soon after you leave, prepare for heavy weather with reefs, harnesses and jacklines, and turn back to the port you left rather than pressing on.
• If you are already well along, choose a harbor ahead that is downwind and has a safe entrance in that wind.
observe: For a novice crew, decide what change would make you shorten or cancel a trip.
Name a sheltered alternative and a return deadline.
sail-20.mistake: Treating a low average wind speed as proof that the entire trip will be safe.

quiz.prompt: The average wind is manageable but the forecast includes strong gusts and worsening visibility. What is appropriate?
options: Depart because only average speed matters
Reassess the trip against crew ability and safe alternatives
quiz.explanation: The entire forecast and its trend matter, not one number.

quiz.prompt: Strong wind is forecast to blow onto the coast you plan to follow. Why is that a concern?
options: It is a lee shore: if something fails, the wind pushes you toward land
It always makes the sea calmer
quiz.explanation: With wind blowing onto the shore you have little room to recover from a failure. Choose a route with more sea room or change the plan.

sail-54.title: Read a weather chart
concepts: A weather chart, or synoptic chart (a snapshot of the whole area at one time), maps air pressure at sea level. Lines called isobars join places of equal pressure, usually every 4 hectopascals (hPa, the same as millibars). A high (H) usually brings settled weather; a low (L) brings cloud, rain and stronger wind.

The closer the isobars, the stronger the wind. Widely spaced isobars mean light wind; isobars bunched together mean a strong blow. Over the sea the wind blows roughly along the isobars, turned a little in toward the lower pressure.

In the northern hemisphere, wind circles a low anticlockwise and spirals in toward its centre, and circles a high clockwise and spirals out. Stand with your back to the wind and the low is on your left. Three other shapes appear on charts:
• A trough is a stretched-out low, bringing cloud and rain like a low.
• A ridge is a stretched-out high, bringing settled weather like a high.
• A col, or saddle, lies between two highs and two lows, with light and changeable wind.

To estimate the wind at a place on the chart, find the isobars there and see which side the low is on. Then draw the wind along the isobars, turned slightly toward the low. With a low to your west, for example, the wind blows from the south, because it circles the low anticlockwise. Once the low has passed to your east, it blows from the north.

A barometer shows the trend, which matters more than the number. Pressure falling steadily, for example from 1000 to 992 hPa in eight hours, means a low is coming closer and the wind will strengthen; a fall of 3 hPa or more in three hours is a warning. Rising pressure after a low usually brings clearing skies and a wind shift. Record the reading in the log every few hours.
observe: Look at a real synoptic chart, find the nearest low and see whether its isobars are close together or far apart.
Note the barometer reading and the time, then compare it three hours later.
sail-54.mistake: Reading one barometer value instead of its trend, or forgetting that wind circles a low anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere.

quiz.prompt: On a weather chart the isobars are close together over your area. What do you expect?
quiz.explanation: The closer the isobars, the stronger the wind.

quiz.prompt: In the northern hemisphere, how does the wind blow around a low?
quiz.explanation: Around a low the wind turns anticlockwise and spirals in; around a high it turns clockwise and spirals out.

quiz.prompt: Your barometer reads 1000, 996, then 992 hPa at four-hour intervals. What does it tell you?
options: A low is approaching and the wind will strengthen
quiz.explanation: A steady fall means a low is coming closer. Watch the trend and expect more wind.

sail-55.title: Fronts and clouds
concepts: A front is the edge where a mass of warm air meets cold air. Most lows that cross the Mediterranean are frontal lows, carrying fronts with them. In the northern hemisphere a warm front usually comes first, then a warm sector, then a cold front, moving roughly from west to east. On a chart a warm front is drawn with half circles, a cold front with triangles.

As a warm front approaches, high thin cloud thickens and lowers into a grey layer, with steady rain, poor visibility and falling pressure. As it passes, the wind veers (shifts clockwise), for example from south to south-west. In the warm sector behind it the isobars are almost straight, the pressure is steady and the air is warm and moist, often with mist or drizzle. Sea fog forms when warm, moist air like this flows over colder water; near the coast it can come and go quickly.

The cold front brings the roughest weather. It builds towering cumulus and cumulonimbus clouds, heavy showers, sometimes thunderstorms and hail, and a sudden, gusty shift of wind to the west or north-west. Behind it the pressure rises, the air is cooler and the visibility improves greatly, though gusty showers can continue.

Cumulonimbus is a cloud of great vertical growth, often with a flat, anvil-shaped top. It can bring squalls, heavy rain, hail and lightning. Clouds form when rising air cools to its dew point (the temperature at which its moisture turns into visible droplets). The cloud base is the height where that happens. Air stops rising once it is no longer warmer than the air around it; forecasters call the air stable at that height.

In a thunderstorm, stay away from the mast, shrouds and other metal fittings. Keep the crew low in the middle of the boat, and switch off electronics you do not need. Reef early, because the squall under a cumulonimbus can arrive with little warning.
observe: Watch how cloud changes over a day: thin high cloud thickening and lowering often means a warm front is coming.
Notice the base of cumulus clouds: it is flat because that is the height where rising air reaches its dew point.
sail-55.mistake: Treating the end of the steady warm-front rain as the end of the bad weather, when the cold front and its squalls are still to come.

quiz.prompt: Which clouds come with a cold front?
quiz.explanation: A cold front lifts air quickly and builds tall cumulus and cumulonimbus, with showers and squalls.

quiz.prompt: After a cold front passes, what usually happens to the visibility?
quiz.explanation: Cooler, drier air arrives behind the cold front and the visibility improves.

quiz.prompt: During a thunderstorm aboard, what should you avoid?
options: Being close to the mast and other metal fittings
quiz.explanation: Lightning follows the mast and rigging. Keep clear of metal fittings and stay low in the middle of the boat.

sail-56.title: Wind and waves
concepts:
The Beaufort scale describes wind by its effect on the sea. Forecasts often give the Beaufort force together with the expected gusts. What each force looks like:
• Force 4 (11–16 knots): many white horses (small breaking crests with white foam).
• Force 5 (17–21): moderate waves and spray.
• Force 6 (22–27): large waves with white foam crests everywhere.
• Force 7 (28–33): a heaped-up sea with foam blown in streaks.
• Force 8 (34–40): a gale.

A sea breeze is caused by the difference in temperature between land and sea. On a sunny day the land warms faster, warm air rises over it, and cooler sea air flows in toward the shore, usually from late morning to evening. At night the land cools and a lighter land breeze may blow out to sea. Mountains make their own winds too: a katabatic wind is cold air flowing down a mountain slope, often strong and dry at the foot of the mountains.

Wind waves are raised by the local wind. Swell is made of waves that were raised by strong wind in a distant storm and have travelled far from it: long, smooth and regular, and they can arrive before or after the storm itself. When the local wind blows against the swell, the swell becomes lower; wind against current, as Lesson {lesson:sail-20} explains, makes waves short and steep.

Waves grow higher and steeper as they reach shallow water, and in a swell they can break across a harbor entrance. Before entering, watch the waves from outside: they often come in sets, with lulls in between. Time your entry for a lull and go in with enough speed to steer.

Breaking waves near the shore can wreck a yacht. Swell from deep water slows and rises when it reaches shallow water, then breaks as a wall of white water. In breaking waves:
• The boat can surf down a wave, dig its bow in and swing out of control (a broach).
• A wave can throw the boat onto rocks, the breakwater or another boat.
• A crew member can be washed overboard, and is very hard to reach in the surf.
The worst position is with the side of the boat to the waves, because a breaking wave can roll it over. Keep the bow or the stern toward them.

The best defence is to stay away from the shore. If the wind and waves are pushing you toward land, act early: set the sails properly or start the engine, and head out to deep water, not closer in. Do not stream a sea anchor near the coast: it holds the bow to the waves, but the boat still drifts onto the beach. If you must come in, choose a harbor that is safe to enter in high seas, even if it is farther away.

To enter through breaking waves:
• Wait outside and watch the sets.
• Approach the entrance head-on, from the direction the waves come from, not along the coast with your side to the waves.
• Put a crew member in the cockpit facing back, to watch the sea behind and call out when a set is coming.
• Right after the last wave of a set, go in with power and get behind the breakwater quickly.
• If a set catches you on the way, turn the bow into the waves and hold there with the engine until it passes. Then turn back and continue in.
observe: Compare the wind instrument with the sea around you and name the Beaufort force from what you see.
On a sunny day, note when the sea breeze starts and how strong it gets by mid-afternoon.
Before entering a harbor in a swell, stop outside and watch a few sets: count the waves in each set and how long the lulls last.
sail-56.mistake: Planning a return in the afternoon on a hot day without allowing for the sea breeze, or rushing a harbor entrance in a swell.

quiz.prompt: The wind gauge shows 25 knots and white foam covers the crests. What Beaufort force is it?
quiz.explanation: Force 6 is 22–27 knots, with large waves and white foam crests everywhere.

quiz.prompt: What causes the summer sea breeze?
options: The difference in temperature between land and sea
quiz.explanation: The land warms faster than the sea; air rises over the land and sea air flows in.

quiz.prompt: What is swell?
options: Waves raised by strong wind in a distant storm
Waves raised by today’s local wind
quiz.explanation: Swell travels far from the storm that made it, so it can arrive even in light local wind.

quiz.prompt: You approach Herzliya marina from the west in a 2 m westerly swell. What is your plan?
options: Expect bigger, breaking waves at the entrance; wait outside and time your entry for a lull
Come in from the north along the coast to check that the entrance is clear
Stream a sea anchor and let the boat drift in slowly
quiz.explanation: The swell grows and may break near the entrance. Coming along the coast puts your side to the waves, and with a sea anchor you still drift onto the shore.

quiz.prompt: Halfway into the entrance, the crew member watching astern calls out that a new set is coming. What do you do?
options: Turn the bow into the waves and hold there with the engine until the set passes, then continue in
Slow down and let the waves carry you in
Turn side-on so the waves pass under you
quiz.explanation: A breaking wave from behind can make you surf and lose control, and side-on is the most dangerous position. Face the set, then go in after it.

quiz.prompt: You sail a 14 m yacht from Ashkelon to Haifa, 2 NM off the coast. Off Tel Aviv a 25-knot south-westerly wind starts. What do you do?
options: Carry on north and shelter in Herzliya marina
Turn in to Tel Aviv marina
quiz.explanation: Herzliya is about 40 minutes away, large and easy to enter before the sea builds. Ashkelon is far away into the wind and waves, and Tel Aviv marina is small, with an entrance that becomes dangerous in a south-westerly sea.

Tel Aviv marina is smaller and waves break earlier near its entrance: the Israeli boat operator licence material advises that in a strong south-westerly wind and sea its entrance is dangerous, so carry on to Herzliya for shelter. Jaffa port is very hard to enter in big waves.

sail-57.title: Eastern Mediterranean weather
concepts: In winter, lows cross the eastern Mediterranean from the west, and some deepen near Cyprus (their pressure drops further, so the wind gets stronger). Along the Israeli coast they usually bring a warm front first, with southerly to south-westerly wind, then a cold front with stormy south-westerly to westerly wind, rising seas and showers. A forecast of a cold front coming in from the sea means rough weather and high waves.

Sharqiya is a strong, dry easterly wind that blows off the land, mainly in spring and autumn. It is felt most in the north of the country. Near the shore the sea stays flat because the wind blows offshore, but farther out it raises waves and can make the return to harbor hard. Winter easterlies are a different case: cold, strong easterly winds in winter usually come from a high pressure system to the north-east, over Russia, not from a low.

In spring, a hot low can move along North Africa or up from the south. Ahead of it the wind is southerly, hot and dry, dust lowers the visibility along the Mediterranean coast, and Eilat gets southerly wind. When it passes, the wind turns west and the temperature drops.

Summer is usually settled: a north-westerly sea breeze builds along the Israeli coast in the afternoon and dies at night. In the Aegean, the Meltemi is a strong, dry north wind in July and August, often force 6 to 7 for days. Farther away, in the Adriatic, the Bora is a cold, dry, very gusty north-easterly wind that falls from the mountains in winter.
observe: Before a passage, read the forecast for the whole region, not just your harbor, and find the nearest low.
On a calm morning with an easterly wind, look offshore: the sea farther out may already be rough.
sail-57.mistake: Leaving on a flat-calm Sharqiya morning, or planning an Aegean summer passage without allowing for the Meltemi.

quiz.prompt: What is the Meltemi?
options: A strong north wind in the Aegean in July and August
A warm south wind in Israel in winter
quiz.explanation: The Meltemi blows from the north across the Aegean in high summer, often force 6 to 7 for days.

quiz.prompt: What is the Sharqiya?
options: A dry easterly wind off the land, mainly in spring and autumn
quiz.explanation: It blows off the land, so the sea near shore is flat while waves build farther out.

quiz.prompt: A winter low is approaching Israel from the west. What usually comes first?
quiz.explanation: The warm front comes first, then the warm sector, then the cold front with the strongest wind and sea.

sail-21.title: Read a practice chart
concepts: A chart is a planning tool, not a picture to follow blindly. Before you use one, check its scale, which way is north, the depths, hazards and marks, and how up to date it is: an old chart can miss a new wreck or a buoy that has moved.

Depths are numbers, usually in metres, and lines called contours join places of equal depth. Shallower water is usually shaded blue, areas that dry at low tide are green, and land is buff or yellow. Measure distance on the latitude scale at the side of the chart: one minute of latitude is one nautical mile.

Buoys tell you where the safe water is and which side to pass. Lateral marks show the two sides of a channel, and each is passed on a set side; cardinal marks show on which side of a danger the safe water lies. Which color goes on which side depends on the region (IALA A or B), so check before you sail. In this app the amber buoys are only practice targets.

In IALA Region A, red marks stay on your left and green marks on your right as you come in from sea.
• Region A covers Europe, Africa, the Mediterranean and most of Asia and Australia.
• Region B, where the colors are the other way round, covers most of the Americas, Japan, Korea and the Philippines.
• Red port-hand marks are cans (flat-topped) and green starboard-hand marks are cones (pointed). Their lights flash in the same color.
A harbor entrance follows the same rule, so a red and a green light close together at night often mark the entrance itself.

Cardinal marks are named after the compass side of a danger where the safe water lies: pass north of a North mark, east of an East mark, and so on. Each carries two black cones on top, and the cones point to where the black is on the mark:
• North: both point up; black over yellow.
• South: both point down; yellow over black.
• East: they point apart; black with a yellow band.
• West: they point together; yellow with a black band.

At night a cardinal mark shows a white quick-flashing light, timed like a clock face. North flashes without stopping; East gives three flashes, like 3 o’clock; South gives six and then one long flash, like 6 o’clock; West gives nine, like 9 o’clock. The long flash keeps a quick count of six from being mistaken for nine. Count a whole group before deciding which side to pass.
observe: Open the chart. Locate north, your position, and the next mark.
Identify land you must keep clear of along the intended route.
sail-21.mistake: Assuming a screen showing your position is a complete and current navigational chart.

quiz.prompt: On a chart, what does one minute of latitude on the side scale measure?
quiz.explanation: Distance is measured on the latitude scale at the side of the chart, level with your position. The longitude scale along the top and bottom changes with latitude, so it is not used for distance.

quiz.prompt: Which should a real chart check include?
options: Scale, source, currency, depths, hazards, and local conventions
quiz.explanation: Charts need interpretation and context to support safe navigation.

quiz.prompt: At night a mark shows nine quick white flashes, then darkness. Where is the safe water?
options: To the west of the mark
To the east of the mark
quiz.explanation: Nine flashes, like 9 o’clock, mean a West cardinal mark: pass to the west of it.
