localNotes: Israel uses IALA Region A. Coming into an Israeli harbor or marina from sea, the flashing green light is on your right and the flashing red light on your left. Leaving the harbor it is the other way round: the green light is on your left and the red on your right.

sail-22.title: Steer toward a waypoint
concepts: A bearing is the direction from your position to a target, such as a waypoint (a planned point you steer for). Check that the direct track, the line you would travel over the ground, is safe and sailable.

A direct bearing may point into the no-go zone (the arc near the wind where sails cannot drive) or cross land. Then plan a different route, such as tacking, rather than forcing the bow toward the target.

Where the bow points is not always where the boat goes. Current and leeway (the wind pushing the boat sideways through the water) push you off course. Aim a little up-current of the mark so the drift carries you onto it, not past it. Check the bearing to the mark now and then: if it keeps changing while you hold your heading, you are being pushed off the line. In this exercise, pass within 35 metres of buoy 1.

A course on the chart is measured from true north, but your compass does not point there. Two errors sit between them:
• Variation: magnetic north is not at true north. The compass rose on the chart gives it for your area, for example 4° East.
• Deviation: the boat’s own metal and electrics pull on the compass. It changes with the heading, so read it from the boat’s deviation card.
Going from compass to true, add errors to the East and subtract errors to the West: True = Compass + Deviation + Variation. Going from true to compass, do the opposite. A memory aid is CADET: Compass ADd East, True. Example: the chart course is 132° true and variation is 4° East, so the magnetic course is 128°. If you must steer 137° by compass to make it good, the deviation is 9° West.
observe: Open the chart before changing course.
Aim toward buoy 1, then check progress and depth regularly.
sail-22.mistake: Fixating on the target and ignoring land, traffic, or the wind angle.

quiz.prompt: Your waypoint lies directly upwind. What is required?
options: Plan a sailable route using tacks
Hold the bow in the no-go zone indefinitely
Increase the compass reading until the wind changes
quiz.explanation: You may need multiple legs to make progress toward an upwind destination.

quiz.prompt: Is the direct bearing always a safe course?
options: Only if the waypoint is visible
No; check hazards, depth, wind, and traffic
quiz.explanation: A bearing describes direction, not safety.

quiz.prompt: The chart course is 100° true. Variation is 3° West and deviation on this heading is 2° East. What do you steer by compass?
quiz.explanation: True to magnetic: a West error is added, so 100° + 3° = 103° magnetic. Magnetic to compass: an East error is subtracted, so 103° − 2° = 101° compass. Check with CADET: 101° + 2° East − 3° West = 100° true.

sail-23.title: Estimate distance and time
concepts: For a first estimate, distance equals speed multiplied by time. At 4 knots, a 3-nautical-mile leg takes 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75 hour, or 45 minutes, if speed remains constant and there is no current.

Dead reckoning advances an earlier position using course, speed, and time. Real estimates also account for current, leeway, and uncertainty; a fix (a position found from landmarks, bearings or GPS, not from your estimate) checks it.
Record assumptions and update the estimate as conditions change. A precise-looking number is not an accurate prediction: an arrival time of 14:37 is still a guess if the current changes.

Keep a logbook, and fill it in regularly. Each entry records:
• where you are: the time, position and log reading (distance run)
• how you move: course and speed
• the weather: wind speed and direction, sea and weather
• events.
If the electronics fail, the last logged position, course, speed and distance let you work out where you are by dead reckoning.
observe: Compute the time for 3 nautical miles at 4 knots before checking the answer.
Describe one reason the actual arrival time might differ.
sail-23.mistake: Mixing minutes and hours or ignoring current and changing boat speed.

quiz.prompt: At 4 knots, how long is a 3-nautical-mile leg without current?
quiz.explanation: 3 ÷ 4 hours = 0.75 hour = 45 minutes.

quiz.prompt: What checks an estimated position?
options: Assuming the log cannot be wrong
An independent position observation or fix
quiz.explanation: An estimate needs verification and an allowance for uncertainty.

sail-24.title: Sail a short passage
concepts: Break a route into legs, the straight stretches between turning points, each with a target, hazards and a plan for the next turn. Look around before turning at a mark, because boats often gather there.
This exercise runs from south of buoy 1 to buoy 1, then buoy 2. The wind makes both direct legs sailable, but you still need to turn and retrim.

Keep at least 3 metres of modeled water depth, because the keel reaches well below the surface and needs a margin. If you run aground, the attempt fails and you start again; passing the marks alone is not enough.
observe: Study both legs before setting off.
At buoy 1, look toward buoy 2 and prepare the course change.
sail-24.mistake: Reaching a waypoint without planning what happens immediately afterward.

quiz.prompt: When should the next leg be considered?
options: Only after leaving the chart behind
Before arriving at the turning point
Never; the yacht follows marks automatically
quiz.explanation: Anticipation leaves time for lookout, crew preparation, and safe course changes.

quiz.prompt: You passed the marks but ran aground. Was the passage successful?
options: No; avoiding hazards is part of the task
Yes, if the speed was high
quiz.explanation: A completed route is not a safe route if essential margins were lost.

sail-25.title: Keep an effective lookout
concepts: A proper lookout uses your eyes, your ears and aids such as radar, AIS (ship tracking) and the radio. The collision rules call this “all available means”. Scan all round, because sails and cabin can hide other boats.

Why a steady bearing means danger: two boats on straight courses that will meet stay at the same angle to each other all the way to the meeting point. So if another vessel stays on the same compass bearing, or stays lined up with the same part of your boat, while it gets closer, you are on a collision course. Check early and repeatedly, and act rather than wait for certainty.
Electronic aids support the lookout; they do not replace it. In the app the other yachts do not move, so it cannot test how well you spot real traffic.
observe: Use the camera to scan the side hidden by the headsail.
Explain how you would share lookout duties with a real crew.
sail-25.mistake: Looking only ahead or only at the chartplotter.

quiz.prompt: A nearby vessel stays at a nearly constant bearing while the distance closes. What might that indicate?
options: No risk because it is not changing direction on the window
A guarantee that it will pass astern
quiz.explanation: Constant bearing with decreasing range is a classic warning; act early based on the full situation.

quiz.prompt: Can a chartplotter replace sight and hearing?
quiz.explanation: Use all appropriate available means and keep an outside lookout.

Check the current Israeli regulations.

sail-26.title: Reason through encounters
concepts: The rules decide in advance who turns away (gives way) and who holds course (stands on), so two boats do not both turn the same way. For two sailing vessels: on different tacks, the port-tack boat (wind coming over its left, port, side) keeps clear; on the same tack, the windward boat keeps clear, because it can usually bear away more easily. Lesson {lesson:sail-46} covers this in full.

An overtaking vessel keeps clear, because the boat ahead may not see it. In a narrow channel, a sailing boat must not block a ship that can only navigate safely inside it; in a traffic lane, it must not block power-driven ships following the lane. Fog, special vessels and local rules can also change who keeps clear. Do not reduce the rules to “sail always wins.”

A stand-on vessel still has responsibilities and must act when needed to avoid collision. If the give-way boat is clearly not keeping clear, the stand-on boat may act on its own; if a collision can no longer be avoided by the give-way boat alone, it must act (Rule 17). A power-driven vessel doing this should, if it can, avoid turning to port for a vessel on its own port side. Learn the full collision rules and local requirements before sailing.
observe: Identify the windward side of each vessel before deciding its tack.
State the assumptions before applying a simplified crossing rule.
sail-26.mistake: Treating stand-on status as permission to ignore developing collision risk.

quiz.prompt: In a basic two-sailing-vessel encounter on different tacks, which normally keeps clear?
quiz.explanation: Under the basic sailing-vessel rule, port tack keeps clear of starboard tack, subject to the full situation and other applicable rules.

quiz.prompt: Does a stand-on vessel have no further responsibility?
options: No; it must continue monitoring and act as required to avoid collision
Yes; it can close its eyes
Yes; the other vessel accepts all responsibility
quiz.explanation: Collision avoidance is an ongoing duty. The complete rules specify stand-on actions and responsibilities.

sail-27.title: Lights, marks, and signals
concepts: Navigation lights show a vessel’s direction and what it is doing. Red is on the port side, green on starboard and white at the stern. See both red and green, and the vessel is heading straight at you, so act now: you may be on a collision course. Red only, you see its port side; green only, its starboard side; white only, you are looking at its stern.

When power-driven vessels can see each other, short horn blasts tell others how they are manoeuvring; these are the international manoeuvring signals. One short blast means “I am turning to starboard”, two mean “I am turning to port”, and three mean “I am running my engine astern (in reverse)”, which does not always mean the boat is already moving backwards. Fog signals are a different system; local or inland rules may differ.

Lesson {lesson:sail-50} covers the full lights, shapes and sound signals. Rules can differ in inland or local waters, so check the rules for where you sail before night or restricted-visibility operation.
observe: Identify the red port light and green starboard light on the yacht.
Distinguish an action signal from a signal used in restricted visibility.
sail-27.mistake: Assuming one memorized signal applies in every jurisdiction and situation.

quiz.prompt: Which side normally carries the red sidelight?
quiz.explanation: The port sidelight is red; starboard is green.

quiz.prompt: In the stated international maneuvering-signal context, two short blasts indicate…
quiz.explanation: Two short blasts from a boat in sight mean “I am turning to port”. Check the rules where you sail before relying on it elsewhere.

sail-61.title: Signal flags and visiting other countries
concepts:
Single flags of the International Code of Signals carry short, urgent messages. Two of them tell you to keep clear:
• Flag A, white and blue with a swallow-tailed (notched) end: "I have a diver down; keep well clear at slow speed." A diver may come up anywhere near the boat.
• Flag B, red and swallow-tailed: the vessel is loading, unloading or carrying dangerous goods such as fuel. Keep clear, though you may still pass or enter a harbor with care. At night she also shows an all-round red light (seen from every direction).

Two other single flags are about people and arriving in port:
• Flag O, red and yellow halves: man overboard. Keep a lookout for a person in the water.
• Flag Q, plain yellow: "My vessel is healthy and I request free pratique." Free pratique is permission from the port health authorities to enter port and go ashore.

Flags N over C, hoisted together, are a distress signal, and so is a square flag with a ball above or below it. A single code flag on its own never means distress. Read a hoist of several flags from the top down. A vessel at anchor may fly a signal flag as well as showing her black ball.

Your ensign, the flag of the country where the boat is registered, flies at the stern. In another country’s waters, also fly that country’s flag, the courtesy flag, under the starboard spreader (the crossbar on the mast). On first arrival, fly the yellow Q flag under the port spreader until customs and immigration have cleared you, then lower it.

Some countries require extra papers for a visiting yacht. Turkey, for example, issues a transit log at an official port of entry, which then allows free movement in Turkish coastal waters. Before you leave, check the entry rules, ports of entry and reporting requirements of every country on your route, and of your own country for the return.
observe: Find the code flags aboard and name what each single flag means.
Before a trip abroad, list the flags you will fly and where each one goes.
sail-61.mistake: Treating a single code flag as a distress signal, or flying a courtesy flag in place of your own ensign.

quiz.prompt: A vessel arriving in port flies a plain yellow flag. What does it mean?
options: My vessel is healthy and I request free pratique
quiz.explanation: Flag Q asks for free pratique, permission to enter port. It comes down once the authorities have cleared you.

quiz.prompt: Where do you fly the courtesy flag of the country you are visiting?
options: At the stern, in place of your ensign
quiz.explanation: The courtesy flag goes under the starboard spreader; your own ensign stays at the stern.

quiz.prompt: A vessel near the harbor entrance flies flag B. What do you do?
options: Enter, but keep well clear of her
Stop and wait outside for permission
quiz.explanation: Flag B means dangerous goods such as fuel. You may pass, but give her plenty of room.

sail-61.transfer: Learn the full International Code of Signals for the waters you sail, and check each country’s current entry rules before you go.

Returning to Israel from abroad, within 25 NM of the coast, report your position and identity to RCC Haifa on VHF channel 16; this entry report is called IMOT. Check the current Israeli regulations.

sail-28.title: Make a passage decision
concepts:
A passage plan answers three questions before you set off:
• Who is going? The crew and their experience.
• What will the weather and water do? The forecast, tides, daylight and the hazards on your route.
• Where can we go if it goes wrong? Safe havens (nearby harbors or bays to shelter in), how you will call for help, and a latest turn-back time.
Good seamanship includes changing or abandoning the plan when its assumptions fail. Do not let an arrival promise outweigh safety, because people under pressure sail on past the easy turn-back point.

Here is how the plan helps you decide when conditions change. You have a novice crew, fading daylight, a forecast wind increase, and an exposed destination. A nearby sheltered alternative is available.
observe: Name the factors that make the original destination less suitable.
Choose a conservative alternative and tell the crew why.
sail-28.mistake: Continuing because the destination was promised before conditions changed.

quiz.prompt: For the stated scenario, which is the sounder decision?
options: Press on to preserve the schedule
Ask the least experienced crew member to decide alone
Reassess and favor the sheltered alternative or an early return
quiz.explanation: Rising exposure and shrinking margins support a conservative change of plan.

quiz.prompt: Which makes an abort plan useful?
options: Clear decision points and viable alternatives
Leaving every decision until the last minute
A promise never to change course
quiz.explanation: Specific triggers and alternatives help avoid rushed decisions under pressure.

sail-29.title: Plan a docking approach
concepts: Docking brings together wind, current, the propeller’s pull, the boat’s momentum (it keeps moving after you slow down) and crew teamwork. Before you start, put out fenders and lines, give each person a job, choose your approach and keep a way out.

Approach into the wind or the current where you can: it slows you down, so you can arrive slowly while water still flows past the rudder for steering. Arrive at the slowest speed that still lets you steer, the speed you would be willing to touch the dock at. Never use a hand or foot to stop the boat.

Two effects catch beginners. In reverse, the propeller pulls the stern to one side (prop walk), so the boat will not back straight at first. And at low speed the wind pushes the high bow away from the dock. Plan for both, and keep a way out. The app models prop walk (try the lab on this page) but not the wind on the hull or dock lines, so docking is taught here as planning.

Most single-engine yachts have a right-hand propeller: seen from astern, it turns clockwise when going ahead. In reverse it walks the stern to port, so the bow swings to starboard; ahead, the effect is weaker and the other way. Use it rather than fight it: in a tight space, turn to starboard, because each burst astern pulls the stern to port and keeps the turn going. Check your own boat in open water, because some propellers turn the other way.

Spring lines run diagonally and stop the boat moving forward or back along the dock. The bow spring runs from the bow aft to the dock, and the stern spring from the stern forward; bow and stern lines hold the boat in. Motoring gently against a spring makes the boat pivot:
• Ahead against the bow spring: the bow is held in and the stern swings out.
• Astern against the stern spring: the stern is held in and the bow swings out.

A spring also gets you off a dock the wind is pushing you onto, where you cannot simply motor sideways away. Put a fender at the bow, motor ahead slowly on the bow spring until the stern is well out, then let go and go astern clear. Alongside another boat of the same size, lie bow to stern so the masts and spreaders cannot touch as the boats roll.

In Mediterranean mooring, the stern or bow is tied to the quay and an anchor or mooring line holds the other end, so many boats fit side by side. Going in stern-to, drop the anchor well out, at right angles to the quay and as far from it as the rode (the anchor chain or rope) allows, then reverse in while paying out. Go in bow-to if the water gets shallow near the quay and could hit the rudder, or for privacy. Some marinas lay a permanent mooring line from a sinker on the seabed, sometimes called a dead anchor: take it to the bow, and when leaving, drop it and let it sink before you use the engine, or it can wrap the propeller.
observe: Describe your approach, crew jobs, and go-around plan before moving.
Explain why wind and current change a safe approach.
sail-29.mistake: Relying on crew to jump ashore or physically catch the yacht.

quiz.prompt: If the approach becomes unstable, what should the preplanned option be?
options: Ask someone to fend off with a foot
Abort and make a controlled new approach if safe
Add speed to get it over with
quiz.explanation: An escape plan is part of preparation; avoid trapping the boat or crew in an unrecoverable maneuver.

quiz.prompt: Why approach a berth heading into the wind or current when you can?
options: It makes the boat go faster
It slows the boat while water still flows past the rudder
quiz.explanation: The wind or current acts as a brake, so you can come in slowly and still steer. With them behind you, the boat keeps being pushed on.

quiz.prompt: With a right-hand propeller, which way does the stern walk when you go astern?
quiz.explanation: A right-hand propeller walks the stern to port in reverse, so the bow swings to starboard. In a tight space, turn to starboard to use it.

sail-30.title: Choose an anchorage
concepts: Choose shelter, holding ground the anchor can dig into (such as sand or mud), and enough depth at every state of the tide. Leave room to swing clear of hazards and other boats.

An anchor holds best when it is pulled flat along the seabed, because then it digs in. With a short rode (the chain or rope between anchor and boat) the pull comes from above and lifts the anchor out. That is why you let out several times the depth: the extra length, and the weight of chain, keep the pull flat and soften jerks from waves. Use more in strong wind. Scope is rode length divided by the height from bow roller to seabed.

Worked example: in 5 m of water with the bow roller 1 m above the water, a 5:1 scope gives 30 m of rode. 5:1 is a common starting point in calm weather; use more in strong wind. Also allow for the tide and check your swing room.

Different anchors suit different seabeds:
• Claw anchors, such as the Bruce, dig well into sand and mud.
• Plough anchors, such as the Delta and CQR, also dig well into sand and mud.
• A folding grapnel suits rock or a small boat.
• A mushroom anchor is meant for permanent moorings in soft mud.
Chain is heavy and keeps the pull low along the bottom. If you use rope, choose one that sinks and stretches, such as nylon: it absorbs jerks and stays clear of propellers. Many yachts use chain with a rope tail.

Sometimes a single anchor is not enough to hold the boat. Use two when one cannot hold in strong wind, when wind and current pull from different directions, or in a river where the current reverses. Lay them well apart, about 45° on either side of the bow in strong wind, or one ahead and one astern in a narrow river, and make sure the rodes cannot tangle as the boat swings.
observe: Sketch the expected swing circle and nearby hazards.
Include roller height in the example’s vertical distance.
sail-30.mistake: Multiplying charted depth alone or assuming an anchor always holds once it touches bottom.

quiz.prompt: Under the stated example assumptions, how much rode corresponds to 5:1?
quiz.explanation: The vertical distance is 5 + 1 = 6 m. Five times 6 m is 30 m, before other real-world considerations.

quiz.prompt: What must an anchorage plan consider beyond depth?
options: Only the distance to a café
Shelter, holding ground, tide, swing room, and hazards
quiz.explanation: Depth alone does not establish a suitable or safe anchorage.

quiz.prompt: Which rope makes a good anchor rode?
options: One that does not stretch at all
quiz.explanation: A sinking rope stays clear of propellers, and its stretch absorbs the jerks of a boat moving in waves.

sail-31.title: Stop, then anchor
concepts: Approach slowly, heading into the wind (or the current, whichever affects the boat more), so the boat comes to a stop on its own. Lower the anchor to the seabed once the boat has stopped. Then let the wind push the boat backward as you pay out rode, so the chain lies along the bottom instead of piling on top of the anchor.

When enough rode is out, set the anchor by pulling on it gently, often with a little engine astern. Check that it holds: pick two objects ashore that line up, such as a lamp post in front of a church tower, and watch whether they stay lined up. Keep checking over time, especially when the wind changes.

You can also feel whether the anchor holds by resting a hand on the rode. A steady pull means it is holding; a juddering vibration means it is dragging across the bottom, and the bow no longer stays pointed into the wind. If it drags, first let out more rode, which often lets it dig in. If it still drags, lift it and anchor again.

Do not leave the anchor’s load on the windlass (the winch that lifts the chain), because it is not built to take sudden jerks. Once anchored, tie a snubber, a short rope from the chain to a bow cleat, so the cleat takes the strain and the rope absorbs jerks. A different use of the anchor: it can help you come close to a shore with the bow facing seaward. Drop it while still approaching and control the rode as it runs out, so the anchor stops the boat under control.

In this exercise: lower the sails and coast below 0.8 knots (slower than walking pace) with the anchor up. Set a 45 m rode target and run the windlass; it pays out over time and stops at the target. Wait for 45 m actually paid out, the windlass stopped, and ground speed below 0.2 knots. Deploying early ends the attempt.
observe: Reduce sail power well before the intended stopping point.
Wait for speed to fall before using the anchor control.
sail-31.mistake: Deploying the anchor at speed instead of completing a controlled approach.

quiz.prompt: What is the correct sequence in this exercise?
options: Anchor at full speed, then lower sails
Lower sails, slow with anchor up, then anchor
quiz.explanation: The exercise checks anticipation and sequencing, not the anchor’s holding ability.

quiz.prompt: Why let the boat drift back while paying out rode?
options: So the rode lies along the seabed instead of piling on the anchor
So the anchor stays off the bottom
quiz.explanation: Rode piled on top of the anchor can foul it. Letting the boat fall back lays the rode out, so the pull on the anchor stays flat.

quiz.prompt: Your hand on the anchor line feels a juddering vibration and the bow falls off the wind. What do you do first?
quiz.explanation: Juddering means the anchor is dragging. More rode often lets it dig in; if it does not, lift the anchor and anchor again.

sail-32.title: Prepare to leave
concepts: Before departure, recheck everything, because things change while you are anchored. A new boat may lie close by, or the wind may shift. Check the route, conditions and crew, secure lines and equipment, and tell everyone what happens next.

To lift the anchor, bring the boat to it rather than pulling the boat with the rode. Motor or sail slowly toward the anchor while the crew brings in the slack. When the rode is straight up and down, the pull is vertical and the anchor breaks out of the seabed easily. The windlass lifts the rode; it is not for towing the boat.

Once the anchor leaves the bottom you are drifting, so get steerage (enough speed for the rudder to work) quickly by engine or sail. Now try it in the app: the bow starts above the anchor. Select Weigh anchor and wait until it is fully stowed, then raise the sails and settle on a steady reach. If the rode goes tight, retrieval pauses.
observe: Confirm the wind and your intended course before releasing the hold.
Restore sail power, gain steerage, and make a controlled departure.
sail-32.mistake: Releasing the boat before having a clear plan and adequate room.

quiz.prompt: What belongs before releasing the boat?
options: Crew briefing, lookout, and a clear plan
Looking at the route only after leaving
quiz.explanation: Preparation should precede the point at which the vessel is free to move.

quiz.prompt: When does an anchor break out of the seabed most easily?
options: When the rode is pulled flat along the bottom
When the rode is straight up and down above it
When the boat moves away fast
quiz.explanation: A vertical pull lifts the anchor’s point out. A flat pull is what makes it dig in, which is why you bring the boat over the anchor first.

Raise sails

sail-33.title: Person overboard priorities
concepts:
When someone falls overboard, act at once, sharing the jobs:
• Shout “person overboard!”
• Throw a lifebuoy and a marker (a buoy with a flag or light) straight away.
• Point at them nonstop: a head in waves vanishes within seconds.
• Call for help and give everyone a job.

Then bring the boat back under control and return. Stay close: many recoveries fail because the boat gets too far away and loses sight of the person. Plan the final approach on a close reach (wind just forward of the side), so you can slow down by easing the sails or speed up by trimming, and stop beside the person. Keep the propeller in neutral or stopped near them.

A lifebuoy light switches itself on when the buoy floats upright in the water, so throw the buoy with its light attached; do not wait to test it. In strong wind and big waves, a return under sail can be hard to control. Once the buoy is thrown and someone is pointing:
• Roll away the headsail.
• Check that no lines are in the water, because a rope can wrap the propeller.
• Start the engine and approach slowly, with the propeller stopped near the person.

Lifting a person aboard is often the hardest part: a wet adult is heavy and the side of the boat is high. Know your boat’s method, such as a sling, a halyard on a winch or a ladder, before you need it. This app has no person-overboard model, so this lesson checks priorities; practice the maneuver with an instructor and a training object.
observe: Assign a dedicated pointer who does not lose sight of the casualty.
Explain why returning alongside is only one part of recovery.
sail-33.mistake: Everyone looking at the controls while nobody keeps the casualty in sight.

quiz.prompt: What is an immediate priority after the alarm?
options: Keep visual contact and deploy appropriate flotation/marking aids
Wait to see whether the person swims back
quiz.explanation: Tracking and supporting the casualty are urgent while the crew organizes the recovery and help.

quiz.prompt: Does reaching the casualty complete the task?
options: No; safe stopping, lifting aboard, and aftercare also matter
quiz.explanation: Recovery includes the difficult physical steps and casualty care, not just navigation.

sail-33.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-34.title: Distress and urgent action
concepts: Distress means grave and imminent danger to life: people need help now. Know the boat’s radio and other communications, the local procedures, and how to give a rescuer four things: who you are, where you are, what is wrong and what help you need.

For an immediate danger to life, use the distress equipment you have. That may be a DSC distress alert (a button on the VHF radio that sends an automatic alert with your position) and a MAYDAY call on VHF channel 16. Learn the equipment before you leave, and never send a real distress alert for practice.

Any one of these signals means a vessel needs immediate help:
• A red hand flare or a red parachute rocket.
• Orange smoke.
• Flames on the vessel.
• The code flags N over C, or a square flag with a ball above or below it.
• A person slowly and repeatedly raising and lowering outstretched arms.
Use them only in real distress, and know where your own flares are and how they fire.

Distress can also be heard, or received by radio:
• A gun or other explosion about once a minute.
• A continuous sound on a horn or fog signal.
• SOS in any signalling method (three short, three long, three short).
• MAYDAY by radio, a DSC distress alert, or an emergency beacon (EPIRB or PLB).
A single code flag on its own is not a distress signal, and other horn patterns, such as six short, three long, six short, mean nothing.

Receiving a distress call obliges you to go and help. Go as fast as you can, unless that would put your own vessel and crew in serious danger, and tell the rescue service what you are doing. Distress means a risk to life. A boat that only wants a tow, with nobody in danger, is not in distress: you may help if your boat, fuel, lines and crew make it safe, but you are not obliged to.

After a grounding, flooding or fire, protect people first. Then work out what has happened, call for help if you need it and follow the boat’s own emergency procedures. Driving hard with the engine after running aground can make the damage worse.

After running aground, first put the engine in neutral. Driving ahead pushes the keel further in and can suck sand into the engine’s cooling water. Check that everyone is unhurt, then check the hull and bilge for water. If the boat is sound, try to come off the way you came: lower or ease the sails so they stop pushing you on, and use reverse gently. If that fails, wait for help or a rising tide rather than forcing it.

When you find water aboard, act at once: start the pumps, then find where the water comes in. Tasting it helps: fresh water points to a tank or pipe, salt water to a hull fitting, hose or damage. Close the seacocks you can reach, and plug or cover the opening with a bung, cloth or cushion held in place. If the pumps cannot keep up, the engine’s sea-water cooling pump can also pump the bilge, on boats fitted to switch its intake. If the water keeps rising, call for help early.

A fire needs fuel, air and heat, so take away any one of them. Turn the boat so the wind carries smoke and flames away from the crew and the rest of the boat; with a fire forward, put the stern to the wind, and with a fire aft, the bow. For an engine fire, stop the engine, shut off the fuel, and discharge the extinguisher through a small opening rather than opening the hatch wide, which feeds the fire with air. Get gas bottles near the fire overboard first.

Locate the simulated position and explain what a real rescue service needs.
sail-34.mistake: Giving a long story but omitting position, identity, or the kind of help needed.

quiz.prompt: Which information is central to a distress message?
options: Identity, position, danger, and assistance needed
quiz.explanation: Clear essential information helps rescuers locate the vessel and prioritize a response.

quiz.prompt: How should you practice an emergency radio message?
options: Make a real distress transmission for realism
Rehearse without transmitting, or use an authorized training setting
quiz.explanation: False distress alerts can divert real emergency resources.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a distress signal?
options: A square flag with a ball above it
quiz.explanation: A square flag with a ball above or below it is a distress signal. A single code flag is not, and five short blasts mean doubt about another vessel’s intentions.

quiz.prompt: Your motorboat runs onto a sandbank. What do you do first?
options: Jump over the side to push
quiz.explanation: Driving ahead pushes you further on and can suck sand into the cooling water. Stop, check people and the hull, then try to back off gently.

sail-62.title: When gear fails, and towing
concepts: If the wheel steering fails, fit the emergency tiller (a steering bar) to the top of the rudder stock, the post that turns the rudder. It is the fix when a steering cable or the wheel’s shaft breaks, and it usually fits under a deck plate in the cockpit. Learn where it is stowed and practise fitting it in calm water. Near a harbor entrance, slow down, call for help early and keep well clear of the breakwater while you fit it.

If the roller furler jams as you roll the headsail away, first take the load off the sail. Bear away so the mainsail shelters it, or ease the sheet, and try again gently. Do not force it with a bigger winch, which can break the drum or the line. If it still will not turn, let the halyard go, pull the sail down onto the deck and tie it there.

If a loaded shroud (a side wire holding up the mast) breaks, act at once to take the strain off the mast. The windward shroud carries the load, so tack or gybe until the broken side is to leeward, ease the sheets and reduce sail. Then rig a spare halyard to a strong point on that side as a temporary shroud before sailing on gently.

Before you take another boat in tow, check the sea state, your fuel and the strength of the points you will tie to on both boats. Use a long, strong line that can stretch, such as 50 m of thick nylon in a 2 m sea; as a rule of thumb, both boats should ride a wave at the same moment. Make it fast to strong points or to a bridle spread across both sides. In rough weather, lengthen the tow line and weight it so it does not snatch tight, and agree signals with the other crew.

Tow slowly and turn gently, because a sharp turn makes the towed boat swing about. With a short line, a sharp turn lets the line go slack. When it comes tight again, it jerks her bow round after you like the end of a whip, so in a sharp turn to starboard she swings hard to starboard and can hit your stern. Turn wide and keep the line taut. In a harbor, towing alongside, lashed to your side, gives far better control.

Look at the shrouds and decide which side carries the load on each tack.
sail-62.mistake: Forcing a jammed furler with a bigger winch, or towing on a short line and turning sharply.

quiz.prompt: When do you need the emergency tiller on a wheel-steered boat?
options: When a steering cable or the wheel’s shaft breaks
Only when the rudder itself breaks
quiz.explanation: The emergency tiller fits straight onto the rudder stock, so it works when the wheel’s link to the rudder fails.

quiz.prompt: On starboard tack, the starboard shroud breaks. What do you do first?
options: Tack so the broken side is to leeward
Hold your course and ease the backstay
Hoist more sail to steady the boat
quiz.explanation: The windward shroud carries the load. Tacking puts the broken side to leeward and takes the strain off the mast.

quiz.prompt: What tow line suits rough weather?
options: A long, heavy line that can stretch
A short line, to keep the boats close
A thin line that will break before the cleats do
quiz.explanation: A long, heavy, stretchy line keeps the boats in step with the waves and stops it snatching tight.

sail-35.title: Your assessed first passage
concepts:
Combine the course skills without rushing, one stage at a time:
• Steer a steady course.
• Trim the sails well.
• Tack, then recover control.
• Slow to a planned stop.

The simulator gives measured targets but no automatic steering. Each stage must be completed in order. Grounding or using the anchor before the final stopping stage invalidates the attempt, because the test checks your order of work, as at sea.

The final stage anchors in deep water, so the target is 180 m of rode. That is far more than the 45 m earlier, because deeper water needs more rode (Lesson {lesson:sail-30}). Wait for all 180 m to be paid out, the windlass to stop, and ground speed to fall below 0.2 knots. Allow about 15 minutes for the complete exercise.

Use the checklist and retain lookout while monitoring the instruments.

quiz.prompt: Which result counts as a successful simulated passage?
options: Completing the stages in order while keeping the safety margins
quiz.explanation: The assessment combines controlled performance, sequence, and maintained margins.

options: Restart, understand the cause, and practice again
Ignore the warning and claim a pass
Change the weather until the result is accepted
quiz.explanation: Reviewing the cause is part of learning; invalid attempts do not earn a pass.

sail-36.title: From simulation to the sea
concepts: Knowing, simulating and doing on a real boat are three different things. Explaining a task, doing it in this model and doing it aboard a real yacht each test something else. Your course record separates theory checks from simulated practice and records the use of hints.

The next step is supervised training on the water, covering:
• preparation and equipment checks

Immediate solo sailing in unfamiliar conditions
Assuming docking and rescue were already mastered
