sail-37.title: Plan the route and the escape
concepts:
A passage plan links preparing, choosing the route, sailing it and checking progress. Check:
• the water: current charts, notices to mariners (official updates on new hazards or moved buoys), tide and current
• the weather: forecast and daylight
• the boat and crew: readiness, ability, fuel and communications
Mark hazards, safe water, alternatives and points where choices become limited.

Choose decision points before you leave, while you still have options. At a decision point you check conditions and choose to go on or divert. In this fictional exercise, the exposed headland is acceptable only if the agreed weather and daylight margins remain. A sheltered alternative is available before the headland; after passing it, returning may be difficult.

Treat the route as a plan you keep checking, not a promise. Compare actual progress and conditions with the plan. Agree a diversion trigger in advance, because it stops you pressing on just because the destination is close. Share the route, crew roles and backup plan.

For a harbor you do not know, read the pilot book, a cruising guide for the area, alongside the official charts. Pilot books describe approaches, anchorages, berthing and mooring arrangements, hazards and local rules. Recent reports from sailors who know the area help too.
observe: Write a primary route, one sheltered alternative and one clear diversion trigger.
Identify the last safe decision point before the exposed section.
sail-37.mistake: Selecting a destination and following its waypoint without checking hazards or preserving an escape option.

quiz.prompt: Before an exposed headland, the forecast worsens beyond your agreed limit. A sheltered alternative remains open. What best follows the plan?
options: Continue because the headland is nearby
Use the sheltered alternative while it remains viable
Increase speed and decide after rounding
quiz.explanation: Act at the planned decision point. Keeping an acceptable alternative avoids committing to conditions beyond the agreed limits.

quiz.prompt: Which makes a contingency usable?
options: A specific trigger, safe alternative and decision point
A promise to reach the destination
A spare waypoint without checking its approach
quiz.explanation: A contingency needs a feasible option and a clear moment to act, checked against conditions and crew capability.

sail-37.transfer: With an instructor, plan a real short passage using current local charts, forecasts and tide information. Walk through the alternatives and the places where turning back becomes difficult.

sail-38.title: Tidal depth and clearance
concepts: Chart depths are measured from a stated low water level called chart datum, so most of the time there is more water than the chart shows. Add the tide height for this place and this time, measured from the same level as the chart. Water depth is not the space under your keel. A depth sounder may measure from the waterline or from the keel, so check its offset (the distance from where it measures to the bottom of the keel).

Here is a worked example with made-up numbers, for a boat that is still and level:
• Charted depth 2.4 m plus tidal height 1.1 m gives a water depth of 3.5 m.
• Take away the 1.8 m draft: 1.7 m of static under-keel clearance (the water between keel and seabed).
• Take away the exercise’s 0.8 m allowance: 0.9 m remains.
This is arithmetic, not permission to cross a shoal.

Real planning needs more margin than this simple sum, for these reasons:
• the tide keeps changing, so use the lowest tide during the passage
• surveys and forecasts are never exact
• waves and heel can bring the keel closer to the bottom
• squat: the boat sits lower when moving fast in shallow water
Do not add the tide again to a depth-sounder reading: it already shows the real water depth. One good reading cannot prove a safe route.
observe: Label chart datum, tidal height, water depth and draft separately in the example.
List information missing before you could approve a real shallow-water passage.
sail-38.mistake: Treating charted depth or a depth-display number as guaranteed under-keel clearance.

quiz.prompt: For the stated example, what is the static clearance before the 0.8 m allowance?
quiz.explanation: Water depth is 2.4 + 1.1 = 3.5 m. Subtracting the 1.8 m draft leaves 1.7 m.

quiz.prompt: Why does that calculation not approve a real crossing?
options: Datum/time, changing tide, uncertainty and dynamic allowances still need checking
quiz.explanation: A static arithmetic result omits changing conditions and uncertainties. Confirm compatible data and adequate vessel-specific margins.

sail-38.transfer: Practice with a current local chart and tide source under instruction. Confirm chart datum, time zone, tidal station, vessel draft and the actual sounder offset before using any number.

sail-39.title: Current vectors and passage time
concepts: Heading is where the bow points; course over ground is where the boat really goes over the seabed. They differ because a current carries the whole boat along, like a moving walkway, so speed through the water and speed over ground differ too. Leeway (sideways slip from the wind) adds another difference. A current's set is the direction it flows toward (setting east carries you east); its drift is its speed in knots.

Fictional example: a current straight along your route simply adds to or takes away from your speed. A yacht makes 5 knots through the water directly along a 12 nautical mile route. A steady 1-knot current directly against the route leaves 4 knots over ground, so the leg takes 3 hours. A current directly behind gives 6 knots and 2 hours. Ignore speeding up and leeway only for this example.

A current from the side pushes you off your line, so you cannot just add or subtract it. Draw the boat's and the current's arrows together: the result is your ground track, and you may need to steer a little into the current to stay on line. Real passages also need:
• current that changes over time
• wind and tacking (zig-zagging upwind)
• sea conditions and a time reserve
So recalculate your ETA (arrival time) from the progress you actually make.
observe: In Boat systems, compare heading and water speed with course and speed over ground.
Draw arrows for a current from ahead, from behind and from the side before doing any sums.
sail-39.mistake: Using water speed for every arrival estimate, or subtracting a cross-current as if it flowed straight along the route.

quiz.prompt: At 5 knots through the water, with a 1-knot current directly against you, how long does the 12 nautical mile leg take?
quiz.explanation: The example gives 4 knots over ground. Time = 12 nautical miles ÷ 4 knots = 3 hours.

quiz.prompt: What changes when the same current flows across the route?
options: Combine the boat's and the current's arrows (speed and direction), then recheck your track and course to steer
Always subtract 1 knot from water speed
Heading and ground track must stay the same
quiz.explanation: A cross-current changes the direction you move over the ground. You can only simply add or subtract speeds when the current flows straight along or against your route, as in the simple examples.

sail-39.transfer: With a navigation instructor and real tidal-stream data, plot a course to steer. Compare planned and actual progress; do not treat this app's current as a local forecast.

sail-40.title: Weather: go, wait or divert
concepts:
Decide before you leave what weather would make you stay in harbour or change plan. That limit belongs to your boat, crew, route and conditions, so a single wind number does not describe the risk. Check official marine forecasts and warnings for:
• gusts (the strongest bursts) and wind direction
• sea state (wave size) and visibility
• where tide or current meets the wind
• a safe alternative route

Fictional decision: if either agreed warning sign is forecast, wait or take the sheltered route. Your crew agreed to avoid an exposed leg if gusts rise beyond its practised ability, or poor visibility hides the pilotage references (marks and landmarks you steer by near the coast). Either is now forecast before you can finish the leg. Waiting, or an acceptable sheltered route, keeps the agreed margin.

Keep checking the weather underway, and change the plan while you still have choices. Wind against current can steepen the waves. An onshore wind raises lee-shore danger (a coast the wind blows toward, so a disabled boat drifts onto it). Reef (make the sail smaller) early as needed and save crew energy. A reef does not make every forecast acceptable.
observe: State two departure limits, and where on the route you would check them again.
Compare the exposed route with its sheltered alternative for wind direction, sea state and visibility.
sail-40.mistake: Treating one wind-speed limit for everyone, or the ability to reef, as proof that a passage is safe.

quiz.prompt: The forecast goes beyond your crew's agreed limits before the exposed leg ends. What is the sound plan?
options: Reef and assume all risk is gone
Ignore the forecast if the harbour is calm
Wait, or choose a checked alternative within the limits
quiz.explanation: The decision to leave should keep the margins agreed for this crew, yacht and route. Calm water in the harbour tells you nothing certain about conditions offshore.

quiz.prompt: Why think about current as well as wind?
options: Wind against current can make the sea steeper and change the route's risk
Current affects only the compass display
quiz.explanation: When wind and current run in opposite directions, the sea can get worse. Look at the route's exposure and the forecast together.

sail-40.transfer: Discuss a real forecast with an instructor, including local effects and how uncertain it is. Agree limits for your own boat and crew, and keep checking them; these examples give no universal safe wind speed.

sail-41.title: Collision risk and limited visibility
concepts: Keep a proper lookout, and treat a steady bearing on an approaching boat as collision risk. Look, listen and use every suitable means available. If an approaching vessel's compass bearing (its direction from you) hardly changes over repeated checks, you are both heading for the same point. A changing bearing does not always remove risk, especially close by, or near a large ship or a tow (a tug pulling something on a long line), whose long length can still hit you. If in doubt, treat risk as present.

Go at a safe speed: one that lets you take avoiding action or stop in time. It depends on:
• visibility and traffic
• how easily your boat turns and stops
• wind, sea and current
• nearby hazards
Act early under the rules and keep checking until the other vessel is past and clear. One AIS symbol (ships shown on a screen by radio) is not a full lookout, because many small boats do not transmit.

When you cannot see the other boat in fog or rain, the usual in-sight give-way rules do not apply (International Rule 19). This holds in or near restricted visibility, because neither boat can see what the other is. Instead:
• slow to a safe speed and keep a lookout
• sound the required signals
• use your equipment correctly
• power-driven vessels keep engines ready to manoeuvre at once
Learn the full rules with an instructor; this exercise picks no universal avoiding turn.
observe: Sketch several compass bearings and distances over time, rather than relying on one glance.
Note what information is missing when a vessel is heard or shown on a screen but cannot be seen.
sail-41.mistake: Claiming an automatic right of way in fog, or assuming that no AIS target means no vessel.

quiz.prompt: A vessel is getting closer while its compass bearing barely changes. What should you conclude?
options: Collision risk exists; keep assessing and act in good time
The other vessel will certainly pass astern
Only motor vessels need to respond
quiz.explanation: A bearing that hardly changes as a vessel approaches is a sign of collision risk. Use all suitable information you have and act under the rules that apply.

quiz.prompt: In restricted visibility, another vessel is not in sight. Which statement is sound under International Rule 19?
options: A sailing yacht always has priority over an unseen motor vessel
Follow the restricted-visibility rules: safe speed and a proper lookout
Keep your speed until you can see the other vessel
quiz.explanation: The in-sight sail and power rules cannot simply be used for a vessel you cannot see. Rule 19 and the general rules call for a response that fits the situation.

sail-41.transfer: Study the full International rules, and any inland or local rules that apply, with a qualified instructor. Practise a steady lookout routine and the use of equipment aboard; this lesson does not test real collision avoidance.

sail-42.title: Night pilotage and cross-checks
concepts: Plan a night approach in daylight: list the lights you expect, in order, and how you will recognize each one. Also mark hazards, safe water, expected depths and a safe alternative. A light is identified by its color, pattern and period: “Fl W 6s” is one white flash every 6 seconds. Time several full cycles; color alone is not enough, and lights ashore can confuse the picture.

Leading lights are two lights, the rear one higher and farther away. When the rear light is straight above the front one, you are on the safe line. If the rear light appears to the right of the front one, you are right of the line: move left until they line up again. Two marks ashore used the same way by day are called a transit.

Cross-check the electronic position with independent evidence such as identified lights, bearings, transits and depth trends. Allow for tide and instrument offsets: the depth sounder may read from the keel, not the surface. Two displays using the same GPS source are not independent fixes. Confirm chart scale, updates and datum (the chart’s reference grid; a mismatch shifts your position); a precise-looking symbol can still be wrong.

When the plotter and what you see disagree, stop and check. In this fictional approach the plotter suggests you are on track, but an expected leading-light alignment and the depth trend disagree. Do not continue into shallower or tighter water just to solve the puzzle. Reduce risk, stay in or return to safe water you have checked if you can, cross-check the observations and revise the plan.
observe: List the expected navigation references in their approach order and explain how each will be identified.
Choose an abort point that leaves adequate sea room before the difficult section.
sail-42.mistake: Trusting a bright plotter symbol over conflicting observations or treating two screens sharing one sensor as independent confirmation.

quiz.prompt: Two screens share the same GPS source. Do matching positions provide independent confirmation?
options: Yes, because there are two screens
Only when both displays are bright
No; use a genuinely independent observation or source
quiz.explanation: A shared sensor can produce the same error on both screens. Identified visual references and properly interpreted depth can provide other evidence.

quiz.prompt: Plotter position conflicts with the expected light alignment and depth trend before a narrow entrance. What is the prudent response?
options: Maintain speed and trust the plotted line
Reduce risk in verified safe water and resolve the disagreement before committing
quiz.explanation: Conflicting observations reduce confidence. Preserve sea room and cross-check before continuing into a constrained approach.

sail-42.transfer: Rehearse a real pilotage plan with an instructor in daylight before supervised night work. Practice identifying light characteristics and obtaining independent position checks.

sail-43.title: Enter the marina under engine
concepts: A boat under engine has no brakes: the only quick way to slow down is reverse thrust, and even that takes time. Ahead (forwards) and astern (backwards) describe the push from the propeller, not which way you are moving; in neutral the push stops but the boat keeps moving. So plan every stop well before you need it.

At low speed little water flows past the rudder, so it steers poorly. A short burst of ahead thrust pushes propeller water straight over the rudder and gives you steering even when the boat is barely moving, without adding much speed. A boat turns around a point near its front, so when you turn, the stern swings out the other way: watch it near pontoons and other boats.

In this exercise: follow the markers on 090° (east), 135° and 180° (south) into the fairway, the open channel between the rows of berths. Stay below 2.5 knots, about walking pace. Then use neutral and a short burst of astern to stop in the final circle, and finish in neutral below 0.15 knots for five seconds, clear of docks and boats.
observe: Use the engine slider or W/S; N selects neutral. Center the helm before overshooting.
Follow the current marker on the chart. The goal panel shows distance, heading, and speed.
sail-43.mistake: Entering too fast and waiting until the stopping circle to reduce power.

quiz.prompt: What should you do before entering the confined fairway?
options: Lower sails and establish a controlled engine approach
quiz.explanation: Prepare the boat and control its speed before entering confined water.

quiz.prompt: What completes the final stop?
options: Reaching the circle at any speed
Holding position and heading at low speed in neutral
quiz.explanation: Position, heading, ground speed, and neutral must all meet the targets for five continuous seconds.

sail-43.transfer: This exercise assesses engine maneuvering in the model. Practice real docking, propeller effects, and mooring lines with a qualified instructor.

steps.label: Enter the approach on 090° at 0.5–2 knots
steps.hint: Apply gentle ahead thrust. Steer east toward the amber marker.

steps.label: Turn into the fairway on 135° at 0.3–1.5 knots
steps.hint: Turn starboard gradually, keeping the dock fingers to port.

steps.label: Stop in the fairway on 180°, neutral, below 0.15 knots
steps.hint: Turn south, slow early, and use astern to check your motion. Return to neutral inside the green circle.

practice.debrief: You entered the marina, turned into the fairway, and stopped under engine control.

sail-44.title: Dock in a marina berth
concepts: Come into a berth (a boat’s parking space at a pontoon) at a speed you would accept touching the dock at, usually walking pace or less. Use short bursts of thrust with neutral between them: each burst gives a little steering and speed, and neutral lets you judge the drift. It is easier to add a little power than to take too much away.

At low speed the wind pushes the boat sideways, and the bow, which is high and light, blows off first. In reverse, most propellers also pull the stern to one side (prop walk), so going astern to stop can swing the stern. Plan the approach so these effects push you toward the berth, not away, and keep a way out if it goes wrong.

In this exercise, approach the amber marker at 0.3–1 knot and continue into the northern berth. To finish, you need:
• position: boat center within 2 metres of the green target
• direction: heading 090° ±10°
• speed: in neutral, below 0.15 knots
• time: held for five seconds
Any contact ends the attempt. In reverse, prop walk swings the stern to port (to the left, looking forward); mooring lines are not part of this model.
observe: The green circle marks the boat center, not the bow. Leave clearance ahead and on both sides.
Watch ground speed and reduce power before reaching the berth.
sail-44.mistake: Using the dock to stop the boat or leaving the engine engaged after reaching the target.

quiz.prompt: Where should the boat stop?
options: With its bow touching the dock
Centered in the marked berth, aligned and clear of obstacles
quiz.explanation: The exercise checks a controlled, aligned stop inside the berth without contact.

quiz.prompt: The boat is aligned but still moving. What is needed?
options: Control the remaining momentum and finish in neutral
quiz.explanation: Alignment alone is insufficient. Slow the boat and hold the complete stopping target.

sail-44.transfer: This exercise assesses engine maneuvering in the model. Practice real docking, propeller effects, and mooring lines with a qualified instructor.

steps.label: Approach the empty berth on 090° at 0.3–1 knot
steps.hint: Use low ahead thrust and keep the bow aligned with the empty northern berth.

steps.label: Park in the berth on 090°, neutral, below 0.15 knots
steps.hint: Slow before the green circle. Use a short astern input, then neutral. Keep clear of the pontoon ahead.

practice.debrief: You maneuvered into the berth and held an aligned stop without contact.

sail-45.title: Leave the berth and exit the marina
concepts: Going backward, the rudder is at the leading end of the boat, so it steers weakly and the opposite way. The same helm turns the bow the other way from going forward. Keep reversing speed low and steady and the helm small, because faster water can force the rudder hard over and swing the bow suddenly. Look where you are going.

Back far enough to clear the dock fingers (the short, narrow pontoons between berths) before you turn. When the boat turns, both ends swing, so turning between the fingers can hit them. Stop, select neutral, then turn under ahead power, where steering is stronger and works the normal way.

In this exercise the lines are already released. Reverse to the first marker on 090° at 0.3–1.2 knots astern, stop at the second target, then use ahead thrust and port helm to turn north and follow the departure markers on 000°. Stay below 2.5 knots and clear of other boats.
observe: Look astern before backing out. Keep the helm centered for the straight reverse leg.
Back far enough to leave turning room, stop, then turn under ahead power.
sail-45.mistake: Turning while still between the dock fingers or accelerating before there is room.

quiz.prompt: When should you start the departure turn?
options: After backing clear and stopping in the fairway
As soon as astern is selected
quiz.explanation: Clear the dock fingers and establish control before turning.

quiz.prompt: How does the rudder respond while moving astern?
quiz.explanation: Water flows the other way past the rudder when moving backwards, so the same helm turns the bow the opposite way.

sail-45.transfer: This exercise assesses engine maneuvering in the model. Practice real docking, propeller effects, and mooring lines with a qualified instructor.

steps.label: Back clear on 090° at 0.3–1.2 knots astern
steps.hint: Select gentle astern with the helm centered. Watch the space behind the boat.

steps.label: Stop in the fairway on 090°, neutral, below 0.15 knots
steps.hint: Use a short ahead input to stop sternway, then neutral. Leave room for the bow to turn.

steps.label: Turn north on 000° at 0.4–1.5 knots
steps.hint: Apply ahead thrust and port helm. Center the helm as the bow approaches north.

steps.label: Exit the marina on 000° at 0.5–2 knots
steps.hint: Continue north toward the final marker, checking heading and keeping a lookout.

practice.debrief: You backed out, stopped clear of the berth, and exited the marina under ahead power.

sail-46.title: Sailing encounters: tack, windward and overtaking
concepts:
Before using the sailing rules, first ask three questions:
• Are the vessels in sight of each other?
• Is there a risk of collision?
• Does overtaking, a narrow channel or a special vessel status change the case?
These sailing examples use International Rules with vessels in sight, in open water, and no special status. Both vessels keep a lookout and remain responsible for avoiding collision.

Port and starboard belong to the boat when facing its bow. A yacht with the wind on its port side is on port tack; wind on starboard means starboard tack. For Rule 12, the windward side is the side opposite the mainsail. Check the mainsail, not just the headsail or where the other yacht appears on your screen.

With collision risk on different tacks, the port-tack yacht keeps out of the way. On the same tack, the windward yacht (closer to where the wind comes from) keeps out of the way of the leeward (downwind) yacht, because it can usually bear away (turn away from the wind) more easily. If you are on port tack and see a vessel to windward whose tack you cannot determine with certainty, keep out of its way. This uncertainty rule is specific; it is not a rule that the yacht seen on your right always wins.

Check overtaking before applying tack rules. You are overtaking when coming up from more than 22.5° abaft the other vessel’s beam (behind the line across its widest point): roughly from behind, in the 135° sector around its stern. At night this corresponds to seeing its sternlight but neither sidelight. Any overtaking vessel keeps clear of the vessel being overtaken, including a sailing yacht overtaking a motor vessel.

If in doubt whether you are overtaking, assume that you are and act accordingly. The obligation continues until finally past and clear. Reaching abeam or changing relative bearing does not turn an established overtaking case into a crossing case.
observe: Identify each yacht’s tack from the mainsail before assigning roles.
Draw the overtaking sector around the other vessel, not your own.
sail-46.mistake: Applying the tack rule before checking whether you are overtaking.

quiz.prompt: You are on port tack; the yacht to windward has an uncertain tack. What is required?
quiz.explanation: Rule 12(a)(iii) requires the port-tack vessel to keep clear in this stated uncertainty.

quiz.prompt: Your sailing yacht is overtaking a motor vessel. When does your duty end?
options: As soon as you are abeam
As soon as your sails fill
quiz.explanation: Rule 13 overrides the simple sail-versus-power comparison and continues through the whole overtaking encounter.

sail-46.transfer: Study the cited International COLREG rules and the rules applicable to your waters. Rehearse these decisions with an instructor; diagrams assess reasoning, not real collision-avoidance competence.

sail-47.title: Under engine: head-on, crossing and mixed encounters
concepts: A boat counts as a sailing vessel only when it is under sail and its engine is not pushing it (Rule 3). A yacht driven by its engine is power-driven even with sails raised. An engine running only to charge batteries does not, on its own, mean the engine is driving the boat. State how the boat is actually being driven before choosing a rule.

When two power-driven vessels in sight cross with collision risk, the one with the other on its starboard side gives way. In plain words: if you see the other boat on your right, you give way, usually by turning right and passing behind it, not crossing ahead if you can avoid it. The other vessel at first keeps its course and speed (Rule 17). Reverse the viewpoint: a contact on A’s starboard can see A on its port side.

When two power-driven vessels with collision risk head straight at each other, bow to bow or nearly so, both turn to starboard. They then pass port-to-port. If both turn right, they always turn away from each other. If in doubt whether this head-on situation exists, assume it does and act accordingly. This is the power-driven head-on rule; do not apply it automatically to two sailing vessels.

In an ordinary in-sight encounter, a power-driven vessel underway keeps out of the way of a sailing vessel. First check the exceptions: narrow channels, traffic lanes and overtaking (Rules 9, 10 and 13), and any special vessel status. A sailing yacht overtaking a motorboat still keeps clear; a yacht using engine propulsion does not claim sailing-vessel status. Vessel size alone does not decide these ordinary encounters.

“Underway” means not at anchor, not made fast to the shore and not aground; a vessel drifting with her engine stopped is still underway. Status matters more than motion: a stopped power-driven vessel that is underway keeps her give-way duties.

Two less common vessels need a second look. A hovercraft running on its air cushion shows an all-round flashing yellow light as well as power-driven lights, and it can be fast. A rowing boat may show sailing-vessel lights or keep a white torch ready to show in time. The International Rules give rowing boats no place of their own in the give-way order, but they are slow and low in the water, so keep clear of them early.
observe: Describe the same crossing from A and B before choosing who acts.
Check whether the engine is actually propelling the yacht.
sail-47.mistake: Treating raised sails as proof of sailing-vessel status while using engine propulsion.

quiz.prompt: Your engine is propelling the yacht and the mainsail is raised. Which status applies?
quiz.explanation: Machinery is providing propulsion, so Rule 3 defines this as a power-driven vessel.

quiz.prompt: Two power-driven vessels meet head-on with collision risk. Who alters course?
quiz.explanation: Rule 14 requires both to alter to starboard for a port-to-port passing.

quiz.prompt: Above a power-driven vessel’s lights you see an all-round flashing yellow light. What is it?
options: A hovercraft on its air cushion
quiz.explanation: Rule 23 gives an air-cushion vessel in non-displacement mode an all-round flashing yellow light. Treat it as a fast power-driven vessel.

sail-47.transfer: Study the cited International COLREG rules and the rules applicable to your waters. Rehearse these decisions with an instructor; diagrams assess reasoning, not real collision-avoidance competence.
localNotes: The Israeli boat operator licence material expects motorboats and sailing boats alike to give way to rowing boats. Check the current Israeli regulations.

sail-48.title: Give-way and stand-on: act as risk develops
concepts: Spot collision risk early, so you know in time whether you must give way or stand on. The give-way vessel must keep out of the way; the stand-on vessel keeps going. Keep a lookout by sight, hearing and all appropriate available means, at a safe speed for visibility, traffic, maneuverability and conditions. A closing vessel on a nearly constant compass bearing (the direction to it) signals risk. A changing bearing does not always rule it out, especially at close range or with large vessels or tows. If in doubt, assume risk exists.

As the give-way boat, act early and boldly so the other boat can see you are keeping clear. Make a large, obvious change of course or speed, because small changes look like no change from the other boat (Rule 8). Avoid a series of small changes. Before you turn, check your sea room (open water around you) and other traffic. If needed, slow down, stop or reverse the engine to avoid collision or to gain time to judge the situation. Then keep watching until you are finally past and clear.

The stand-on boat's duty grows in three stages as the danger grows (Rule 17). Start weighing your options early; do not wait for the last stage. The stages:
• At first, keep your course and speed, so the other boat can predict you.
• Once it is clear the give-way boat is not acting properly, you may act on your own.
• When so close that the give-way boat alone can no longer avoid collision, you must act in the way that best helps avoid it.

When two power boats cross and you stand on but act, avoid turning left (to port) toward a boat on your left. This applies when two power-driven vessels cross and you, the stand-on boat, act alone because the other is not giving way (Rule 17(a)(ii)). Where possible, do not alter to port for a vessel on your own port side, because if she does finally turn to starboard (right), as the rules expect, your turn to port would carry you into her. This is a specific limit, not an order to turn right in every emergency. The give-way vessel must still keep clear even when you act.

There is no fixed safe passing distance, so judge each situation and keep checking. There is also no last-second turning point that always works. You stay responsible for ordinary good seamanship and for special circumstances (Rule 2). You may break a rule only when you must, to avoid a danger that is about to happen (Rule 2). Being the stand-on boat never gives you an unconditional right to collide.
observe: Describe what changes for the stand-on boat between “may act” and “must act.”
After a maneuver, check the new bearing, the range (distance) and the surrounding traffic.
sail-48.mistake: Keeping course and speed as the stand-on boat when the other vessel alone can no longer prevent a collision.

quiz.prompt: The give-way vessel is clearly not acting properly. May the stand-on vessel act before collision becomes unavoidable by the give-way vessel alone?
quiz.explanation: The permission to act comes earlier than the final duty to act. Keep judging the full situation.

quiz.prompt: You have made a turn to avoid another vessel. What completes the response?
options: Check that it works until you are past and clear
Assume the turn removed every risk
quiz.explanation: Rule 8 requires you to check the effect of your maneuver and pass at a safe distance, without creating another close-quarters situation.

sail-48.transfer: Study the cited International COLREG rules and the rules applicable to your waters. Rehearse these decisions with an instructor; diagrams assess reasoning, not real collision-avoidance competence.

sail-49.title: Special vessels, narrow channels and traffic lanes
concepts:
Judge a vessel by what it can actually do, not by how big it looks. Confirm her status from the right lights, shapes and the situation. Three special kinds matter here:
• Not under command: exceptional circumstances (such as a steering failure) stop her maneuvering as the rules require.
• Restricted in ability to maneuver: her work, such as dredging, limits how she can follow the rules.
• Engaged in fishing: her gear (nets or lines) limits her maneuvering; recreational trolling that does not do this does not count.

Vessels that cannot easily turn or stop get room from vessels that can. An ordinary sailing vessel underway (not anchored, tied up or aground) keeps clear of vessels not under command, restricted in ability to maneuver, and engaged in fishing. An ordinary power-driven vessel (one using an engine) also keeps clear of sailing vessels. Narrow channels, traffic lanes and overtaking can change this order (Rules 9, 10 and 13). A vessel constrained by her draught (a deep ship that must stay in deep water) shows special signals. All vessels except those not under command or restricted in ability to maneuver should, where possible, avoid impeding her (getting in her way) by moving early (International Rule 18(d)). She still navigates with particular caution. When both vessels have a special status, for example one not under command and one restricted in ability to maneuver, the rules give neither priority, so both act to avoid collision.

In a narrow channel, keep as near the starboard (right-hand) edge as is safe and practicable. A sailing vessel or a vessel under 20 m (about 65 feet) must not impede a vessel that can safely navigate only within the channel, because the big ship has nowhere else to go (Rule 9). Do not cross if that would impede such a vessel. Fishing vessels must not impede other vessels navigating the channel. Approach bends you cannot see around with particular alertness and caution. Where possible, do not anchor in the channel.

A traffic separation scheme is a set of one-way shipping lanes, like a motorway, so follow your lane's direction. These schemes, adopted by the International Maritime Organization (IMO), have a central strip between lanes, the separation zone. Join or leave a lane from the side at a small angle. Avoid crossing if you can. If you must cross, keep your heading (where your bow points) as nearly as practicable at right angles to the traffic flow, so you leave the lane fastest and ships see clearly what you are doing. This means heading, not a ground track corrected for current. Sailing vessels and vessels under 20 m must not impede power-driven vessels following a lane. Stay out of separation zones except as the rules allow (Rule 10).

“Do not impede” means acting early to leave plenty of sea room, before any risk of collision develops. The duty continues if risk does develop, and both vessels must then also follow the collision-avoidance rules. A traffic lane does not give a ship an unconditional right of way. Check local harbor directions, charts and notices as well as the International Rules.

In a narrow channel, ask by whistle before overtaking (passing a slower vessel ahead). You do this when you can pass safely only if the vessel ahead moves over. A prolonged blast lasts 4 to 6 seconds; a short blast about 1 second. The signals (Rule 34(c)):
• Two prolonged, one short: “I intend to overtake you on your starboard side.”
• Two prolonged, two short: “I intend to overtake you on your port (left) side.”
• Prolonged, short, prolonged, short: the vessel ahead agrees and makes room.
• At least five short rapid blasts: the vessel ahead doubts it is safe.

A dredger or underwater work vessel shows which side is blocked and which side you may pass. Her work may block one side. On the blocked side she shows two all-round red lights (seen from every direction), or two black balls by day. On the side where you may pass, she shows two all-round green lights, or two black diamonds by day. These come with her red-white-red lights or ball-diamond-ball shapes, the signal for restricted in ability to maneuver.

Fishing gear reaching more than 150 m out is marked on the side where it extends. 150 m is about one and a half football pitches. As well as her fishing lights, the vessel shows an all-round white light, or by day a cone point up, in the direction of the gear. Pass on the other side, well clear of the gear, because nets and lines can catch your keel or propeller.
observe: Tell apart a vessel restricted by her work from one that is simply large.
For a traffic-lane crossing, compare your heading with your course over ground (your actual path, which current can push sideways).
sail-49.mistake: Using “sail has priority” as a reason to cross ahead of a ship that can navigate safely only in the channel.

quiz.prompt: Your sailing yacht would impede a ship that can safely navigate only in this narrow channel. What is required?
options: Act early so you do not impede its passage
quiz.explanation: Rule 9 requires a sailing vessel not to impede such a ship; this duty does not depend on a radio call.

quiz.prompt: When you must cross a traffic lane, what should be nearly at right angles to the traffic flow?
quiz.explanation: Rule 10(c) specifies heading. Current can make your track over the ground differ.

quiz.prompt: In a narrow channel, the vessel ahead hears two prolonged and two short blasts from astern (behind). What do they mean?
options: The vessel astern intends to overtake on the port side
The vessel astern is in distress
The vessel astern intends to overtake on the starboard side
quiz.explanation: Under Rule 34(c), two prolonged and one short ask to pass on the starboard side; two prolonged and two short, on the port side. The vessel ahead agrees with prolonged-short-prolonged-short, or sounds five short blasts if in doubt.

sail-49.transfer: Study the cited International COLREG rules and the rules applicable to your waters. Rehearse these decisions with an instructor; diagrams assess reasoning, not real collision-avoidance competence.
localNotes: In the narrow Gulf of Eilat, a yacht must keep clear of a large ship that can navigate only within the channel, even though at open sea a power-driven vessel gives way to sail.

sail-50.title: Read lights, shapes and sound signals
concepts: Each light shines over only part of the circle, so the lights you see show which way a boat faces. Red is the port (left) sidelight and green the starboard (right) one. Each covers 112.5°, from dead ahead to 22.5° abaft the beam (just behind the side). The white sternlight covers the remaining 135° astern; the white masthead light covers 225° ahead. Red and green together mean she is heading at you. One white light alone might be a sternlight, anchor light or another permitted light: it proves neither vessel type nor absence of risk.

A boat's normal lights and shapes depend on what she is doing:
• Sailing vessel: sidelights and a sternlight (small-vessel options and exceptions depend on length).
• Power-driven vessel: adds the required masthead light or lights.
• Under sail and engine together: a black cone, point down, by day.
• At anchor: the required all-round white light or lights (seen from every direction), and a black ball by day, with length and location exceptions.
A sailing vessel may also show an optional pair of all-round lights at the masthead, red over green (“red over green, sailing machine”). She may not show them together with a combined masthead lantern (red, green and white in one lantern at the top of the mast). Study the complete arrangements before sailing at night.

Some lights and shapes show a special status; read them from top to bottom:
• Not under command (cannot maneuver as needed): two all-round red lights, or two black balls by day.
• Restricted in ability to maneuver (her work limits her movement): red-white-red, or ball-diamond-ball.
• Fishing other than trawling: red over white.
• Trawling (dragging a net): green over white.
• Constrained by draught (too deep to leave deep water): three all-round red lights, or a cylinder.
Fishing day shapes are two cones with points together. These are status signals, so navigation lights may also be needed. The next pages add large, anchored, aground, towing, pilot and diving vessels.

Lights are shown from sunset to sunrise and whenever visibility is restricted. That includes daytime fog or heavy rain. Shapes are shown by day. During those hours, show no other lights that could be mistaken for navigation lights or spoil the lookout, because they can hide the real pattern. An ordinary yacht or motorboat with no special status has no day shape to show.

Large power-driven vessels show two masthead lights, which also show which way they point. A power-driven vessel 50 m or longer (about the length of an Olympic pool) shows two, the after (rear) one higher than the forward one. When the two lights line up vertically, she is pointing toward you or away from you. A vessel under 50 m may show only one. A vessel restricted in ability to maneuver adds masthead lights, sidelights and a sternlight to her red-white-red only while making way (actually moving through the water).

Anchored vessels show all-round white lights at night and one black ball by day. A vessel under 50 m shows one all-round white light where it can best be seen. A vessel of 50 m or more shows two: one forward and a lower one at or near the stern. The black ball is shown forward. A vessel of 100 m or more also lights her decks, so a brightly lit ship that is not moving may well be at anchor.

A vessel aground warns you about the ship and about shallow water nearby. A vessel aground (stuck on the bottom) shows her anchor lights plus two all-round red lights in a vertical line; by day, three black balls in a vertical line. The depth there was too little for her, so it may be too little for you.

A towing vessel adds masthead lights and a yellow towing light. A power-driven vessel towing astern (pulling the tow behind her) shows two masthead lights in a vertical line. She shows three when the tow is longer than 200 m (about two football pitches), measured from her stern to the end of the tow. She also shows sidelights, a sternlight and a yellow towing light above the sternlight. The towed vessel shows sidelights and a sternlight. Only when the tow is longer than 200 m do both show a black diamond by day. Never pass between a tug and its tow, because the towline can be hidden low in the water.

An ordinary tug and tow is a power-driven vessel, so it keeps out of the way of a sailing vessel. It follows the normal crossing and head-on rules. A vessel pushing ahead or towing alongside (the tow tied to her side) shows two masthead lights, sidelights and a sternlight, but no yellow towing light. If towing work severely restricts her ability to change course, the tug also shows red-white-red, or ball-diamond-ball by day. Then other vessels, including sailing vessels, keep out of her way.

A pilot vessel on duty shows two all-round lights at the masthead, white over red. A pilot is a local expert who boards ships to guide them in; a memory aid is “white over red, pilot ahead.” Underway (not anchored, moored or aground), she adds sidelights and a sternlight; at anchor, her anchor lights. Ships slow down and maneuver near a pilot station to take on a pilot, so expect sudden changes there.

A vessel supporting divers shows code flag A by day and red-white-red at night. The flag is a rigid copy at least 1 m high, white and blue with a swallow-tailed end (a V-shaped notch at the free end). At night she shows the restricted-in-ability-to-maneuver lights, red-white-red. Divers may be in the water anywhere around her, so keep well clear and slow down.

Power-driven vessels that can see each other signal their maneuvers with horn blasts:
• One short blast: altering to starboard.
• Two short blasts: altering to port.
• Three short blasts: operating astern propulsion (engine in reverse).
• At least five short rapid blasts: doubt about the other's intentions, or whether she is doing enough.
A short blast lasts about one second; a prolonged blast, four to six seconds. These come from a power-driven vessel underway, maneuvering with vessels in sight (International Rule 34). Three blasts do not necessarily mean she is already moving backward. Near a blind channel bend, sound one prolonged blast; an approaching vessel within hearing answers with one prolonged blast.

In fog, vessels sound a different set of signals, at intervals of no more than two minutes. A power-driven vessel making way sounds one prolonged blast. Underway but stopped and making no way, she sounds two prolonged blasts about two seconds apart. A manned towed vessel, the last of the tow, sounds one prolonged and three short right after the tug's signal. One prolonged then two short is sounded by:
• a sailing vessel
• a vessel not under command, or restricted in ability to maneuver
• a vessel constrained by draught, or engaged in fishing
• a vessel towing or pushing
So that signal does not identify a sailing vessel alone. Rule 35 specifies other cases and small-vessel exceptions; International and inland signals can differ.

Reading the lights is only the first step; then decide who keeps clear. Work through it in order:
• Name the vessel from her whole pattern of lights or shapes.
• Note which side of her you see: green is her starboard side, red her port side, and both together mean she is heading at you.
• Check your own status too. With the engine running you are power-driven, even with the sails up, so you keep clear of a sailing vessel; by day show the cone, point down. If you are not under command yourself, show your two red lights or two black balls and others keep clear of you. Two vessels with special status, such as not under command and restricted in ability to maneuver, both act to avoid collision.
• The usual order (Rule 18): a power-driven vessel keeps clear of a sailing vessel; a sailing vessel keeps clear of vessels fishing, restricted in ability to maneuver or not under command; and both avoid impeding a vessel constrained by her draught. Overtaking, narrow channels and traffic lanes come first.
If you are the stand-on vessel, hold your course and speed but keep watching, and act if the other vessel does not.
observe: Name the full observed light pattern before inferring vessel status.
Separate in-sight maneuvering signals from fog signals.
sail-50.mistake: Identifying a vessel from one color or treating a fog signal as a turning instruction.

quiz.prompt: Two vessels can see each other. Under International Rule 34, three short blasts mean…
quiz.explanation: The signal says her engine is working astern (in reverse). It does not guarantee she is already moving backward through the water.

quiz.prompt: In fog you hear one prolonged and two short blasts. What can you conclude?
options: Several categories use this signal; identity remains uncertain
quiz.explanation: Under Rule 35, sailing vessels and several special vessel types all use this pattern. Keep assessing the risk.

quiz.prompt: At night you see white anchor lights and two all-round red lights in a vertical line. What is it?
options: A vessel not under command making way
quiz.explanation: Anchor lights plus two vertical reds mean aground; by day she shows three black balls. Expect shallow water nearby.

quiz.prompt: A tug and the vessel she tows both show a black diamond by day. What does the diamond tell you?
options: The tow is longer than 200 m
The tug is restricted in ability to maneuver
quiz.explanation: Rule 24 adds the diamond, and a third masthead light at night, only when the tow is longer than 200 m. A shorter tow needs no day shape.

sail-50.transfer: Study the cited International COLREG rules and the rules applicable to your waters. Rehearse these decisions with an instructor; diagrams assess reasoning, not real collision-avoidance competence.
localNotes: The Israeli boat operator licence material expects you to keep at least 200 m from a vessel showing the diving flag. Check the current Israeli regulations before you rely on a distance.

sail-51.title: Restricted visibility and a complete encounter plan
concepts: First decide which set of rules applies; only then decide who gives way. When vessels cannot see each other and are in or near restricted visibility (fog, heavy rain or similar), International Rule 19 applies. Then do not give an unseen contact (a vessel detected but not seen) the ordinary in-sight roles, such as sail before power or the crossing rules. If you can see each other, use the in-sight rules, still allowing for the visibility and your general duties.

In poor visibility, go at a safe speed and keep a lookout, so you can stop or turn in time. A power-driven vessel keeps engines ready for immediate maneuver. Use the required sound signals and your equipment correctly. Avoid conclusions from scanty radar information: one or two glimpses cannot show another boat's course. AIS (ships broadcasting position and course) and radio do not replace lookout, give a complete traffic picture or cancel the rules.

If a vessel shows only on radar, judge the risk early and act in good time. Work out whether close quarters (getting dangerously close) or collision risk is developing. If you alter course, as far as possible do not turn to port (left) for a vessel forward of the beam (ahead of your side), unless you are overtaking her. Also avoid turning toward a vessel abeam or abaft the beam (beside or behind you) (Rule 19(d)). No single turn is always safe, so check all contacts, sea room (space to maneuver) and speed options.

If a fog signal seems to come from forward of the beam, slow right down. Go at the lowest speed that still keeps your course. Do the same if you cannot avoid getting close to a vessel forward of the beam. This applies unless you are already sure there is no risk of collision. Take all way off (stop in the water) if needed, and navigate with extreme caution until the danger is over (Rule 19(e)). Do not hold cruising speed waiting to see the vessel, because you cannot yet tell where she is going.

Use the same five steps in every exercise, in this order:
• Observe and assess the risk.
• Establish the visibility, how each vessel is driven, her status and local limits.
• Check for overtaking before the ordinary encounter roles.
• Choose timely action that does not create another danger.
• Keep checking the result until you are past and clear.
Start the assessment again whenever conditions change. These lessons teach core International encounter reasoning, not the complete lights syllabus, local law or a qualification for unsupervised navigation.
observe: State explicitly whether the contact is visually in sight or detected only by instruments.
Reassess a closing contact after each new observation; a plan alone does not remove risk.
sail-51.mistake: Assigning automatic sailing priority to a contact that is not in sight in fog.

quiz.prompt: In fog, another vessel is detected by radar but not seen. Which framework applies?
options: Rule 19 plus the general duties that apply
No rules until you can see her
quiz.explanation: The rules for vessels not in sight in restricted visibility apply; you cannot simply assign the ordinary in-sight roles.

quiz.prompt: A fog signal seems to come from forward of your beam, and you have not made sure there is no risk. What must you do?
options: Keep speed until you see the vessel
Turn to port immediately in every case
Slow to the lowest speed that keeps your course; take all way off if needed
quiz.explanation: Rule 19(e) requires this slowdown and extreme caution until the danger of collision is over.

sail-51.transfer: Study the cited International COLREG rules and the rules applicable to your waters. Rehearse these decisions with an instructor; diagrams assess reasoning, not real collision-avoidance competence.

sail-52.title: Handle a catamaran with twin engines
concepts: A cruising catamaran has two widely spaced hulls and engines. Allow for its beam (its width, much wider than a monohull of the same length) when choosing a berth or turning space. Shallow draft does not guarantee clearance; check the actual vessel, depth, and margins. High topsides (the hull sides above the water) and a wide cabin can catch the wind at low speed.

The engines are far apart, so each one pushes on a long lever: opposite thrust spins the boat almost on the spot. Equal engine commands give mainly ahead or astern motion. With the helm centered, port ahead and starboard astern turn the bow to starboard; reverse the commands to turn to port. Use gentle bursts with neutral between them. Equal lever settings need not produce equal ahead and astern thrust, so watch both heading and drift.

This exercise starts in open water with sails lowered. Use the separate port and starboard engine controls to turn from 000° to 090° within the starting circle. Stop the rotation and select neutral on both engines for five seconds. Then use the linked engine control to reach the next marker and stop in the final circle. Stay below 2.5 knots and clear of traffic.

Under sail, a catamaran may heel little even as loads increase. Reef early using the boat maker’s guidance, forecast, sea state, and crew ability. Wide beam gives initial stability, not immunity from capsize. Low heel is not permission to carry more sail: a monohull leans to warn you, but a catamaran gives little warning before a capsize, and then stays upside down.
observe: Keep the helm centered for the pivot; use opposing engines and ease before 090° to allow for momentum.
N or the linked neutral control stops both engines. Opposing engine commands are not neutral, even if their average is zero.
sail-52.mistake: Relying on the rudder at rest, or assuming low heel means low sail loads.

quiz.prompt: With the helm centered, which engine combination turns the bow to starboard?
quiz.explanation: One engine pushes forward and the other back, so the boat spins. Watch drift because ahead and astern thrust may differ.

quiz.prompt: The wind is increasing but the catamaran is hardly heeling. What should guide reefing?
options: Wait for a large heel angle
The boat maker’s guidance, conditions, loads, and crew ability
quiz.explanation: Low heel can hide increasing loads. Catamarans have finite stability and need timely sail reduction.

sail-52.transfer: Practice on the specific catamaran with a qualified instructor. This model does not assess real windage, propeller wash, mooring lines, or capsize recovery.

steps.label: Pivot to 090° and hold neutral below 0.15 knots
steps.hint: Center the helm. Use port ahead and starboard astern gently. Ease early, check the turn, and select neutral on both engines.

steps.label: Proceed on 090° at 0.5–1.5 knots
steps.hint: Use the linked engine control for equal ahead thrust. Keep the bow east and watch the marker.

steps.label: Stop on 090° with both engines neutral
steps.hint: Reduce power early. Use brief astern thrust to check headway, then neutral. Hold below 0.15 knots for five seconds.

practice.debrief: You turned a twin-engine catamaran, made a controlled approach, and stopped with both engines neutral.

sail-53.title: Navigate a night approach
concepts: At night you recognize a light by its color, its pattern and its period, the time for one full cycle. Watch two or three complete cycles and count, then match them with the chart. Color alone is not enough: there are many white lights ashore. Protect your night vision: dim the screens and use red light in the cockpit.

Leading lights are two lights, the rear one higher and farther away, used as in Lesson {lesson:sail-42}. When the rear light is straight above the front one, you are on the line. If the rear light appears to the right, you are right of the line: move left until they line up again. If they never line up where you expect, slow down, stay in safe water and check you have the right lights. Cross-check with heading, chart position and depth.

In this exercise (fictional lights) the lighthouse flashes white every 6 seconds and buoy 1 flashes yellow every 4 seconds. Stay below 3 knots and in at least 3 metres of water:
• steer 000° with gentle ahead thrust
• pass east of buoy 1
• turn onto the leading line on 027°
• slow, use a brief astern input, and hold below 0.15 knots in neutral on 027° for five seconds
observe: Watch the white lighthouse for two complete 6-second cycles before setting off. The beacons pause when the simulation is paused.
Use W/S or the engine slider for thrust and N for neutral. Make small helm corrections; the chart and goal panel show the next checkpoint.
sail-53.mistake: Identifying a light by color alone or reaching the stopping circle before reducing speed.

quiz.prompt: Which observation identifies the lighthouse in this exercise?
options: A white flash once every 6 seconds
A yellow flash once every 4 seconds
quiz.explanation: Match the color and the complete flash period with the training light list.

quiz.prompt: What completes the final checkpoint?
options: Holding the marked position and heading below 0.15 knots in neutral
quiz.explanation: Position, heading, speed and neutral must meet the targets together for five continuous seconds.

sail-53.transfer: Practice real night pilotage with an instructor using current charts and light lists. This exercise does not reproduce dark adaptation, visibility limits or every vessel-light configuration.

steps.label: Review the chart and light characteristics
steps.hint: Open the chart. Find Fl W 6s, buoy 1 (Fl Y 4s), and the steady white leading lights on 027°.

steps.label: Approach buoy 1 on 000° at 0.5–2.5 knots
steps.hint: Use gentle ahead thrust and steer north. Keep the yellow buoy to port and compare its 4-second flash with the chart.

steps.label: Join the leading line on 027° at 0.5–2 knots
steps.hint: Turn gradually toward 027°. Align the two steady white lights ahead; confirm your depth and chart position.

steps.label: Stop on 027°, neutral, below 0.15 knots
steps.hint: Slow early. Use a short astern input, then neutral in the final circle. Hold position and heading for five seconds.

practice.debrief: You reviewed the light list, steered a night approach, joined the leading line and stopped in safe water.
